records.transcript: Today we're going to look at Cubism, one of the most influential artistic movements of the early twentieth century. Cubism is closely associated with Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, but its importance goes beyond the work of those two painters. It changed how artists thought about representation itself. For centuries, much European painting had tried to create the illusion of looking through a window. An object was normally shown from one fixed viewpoint, with perspective used to make the space look realistic. Cubist artists questioned that convention. They asked: Why should a painting show an object from only one position when, in real life, we understand an object by moving around it and seeing it from many directions? Imagine a coffee cup sitting on a table. From the side, you see the handle clearly, but the circular opening at the top appears compressed. From above, the opening looks circular, while the handle changes shape. A Cubist artist might combine several of those views in a single image. The cup could be broken into geometric planes and then reorganized so that different sides seem visible at the same time. That's why Cubist paintings can initially look fragmented or distorted. And when Cubism first appeared, not everyone admired it. Some critics thought the paintings looked unfinished, confusing, or even ugly. The rejection of normal perspective seemed to them like a rejection of artistic skill. But Cubism turned out to be enormously influential. It encouraged later artists to think of a painting not simply as a picture of reality but as an independent arrangement of shapes, lines, and surfaces. Its influence spread into sculpture, graphic design, architecture, and other visual fields. This is one reason Cubism is so important to the broader history of Modernism. Modernist artists and designers were experimenting with new forms and questioning inherited traditions. Cubism became one of the clearest demonstrations that even something as basic as visual perspective could be rethought. So the movement mattered not only because Picasso and Braque created unusual paintings. Cubism helped transform expectations about what art could do, and its effects continued long after the first Cubist works stopped shocking the public.
records.translation:
今天我们将探讨立体主义，它是二十世纪初最具影响力的艺术运动之一。
立体主义与巴勃罗·毕加索和乔治·布拉克密切相关，但其重要性超越了这两位画家的作品。
它改变了艺术家对再现本身的看法。
几个世纪以来，许多欧洲绘画都试图创造透过窗户看东西的幻觉。
物体通常从一个固定的视角展示，并使用透视法使空间看起来真实。
立体派艺术家质疑了这一传统。
他们问道：为什么一幅画只能从一个角度展示一个物体，而现实生活中，我们通过围绕物体移动并从多个方向观察它来理解它呢？
想象一个放在桌子上的咖啡杯。
从侧面看，你能清楚地看到把手，但顶部的圆形开口看起来是扁平的。
从上方看，开口是圆形的，而把手则改变了形状。
一位立体派艺术家可能会将这些不同的视角组合在一幅画中。
杯子可以被分解成几何平面，然后重新组织，使不同的侧面似乎同时可见。
这就是为什么立体派绘画最初看起来支离破碎或扭曲的原因。
当立体主义首次出现时，并不是所有人都欣赏它。
一些评论家认为这些画看起来未完成、令人困惑，甚至丑陋。
对正常透视的拒绝在他们看来是对艺术技巧的拒绝。
但立体主义最终产生了巨大的影响。
它鼓励后来的艺术家将绘画不仅仅视为现实的图画，而是形状、线条和表面的独立排列。
它的影响传播到雕塑、平面设计、建筑和其他视觉领域。
这也是立体主义对更广阔的现代主义历史如此重要的原因之一。
现代主义艺术家和设计师正在尝试新的形式并质疑传统。
立体主义成为最清晰的证明之一，即即使是像视觉透视这样基本的东西也可以被重新思考。
所以这项运动之所以重要，不仅仅是因为毕加索和布拉克创作了不同寻常的画作。
立体主义帮助改变了人们对艺术能做什么的期望，它的影响在第一批立体主义作品不再震惊公众之后很久仍在继续。

records.transcript: Isolation appears in many novels, but authors can use it in very different ways. Today I want to look at how isolation is represented through individual characters and how it can shape what those characters become. Let's begin with Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein*. The creature is isolated largely because of his appearance. People react to him with fear before they learn anything about his personality. He wants companionship and initially tries to observe and understand human society, but repeated rejection turns him into an outcast. So in this case, isolation is imposed from the outside. His appearance causes other people to exclude him. Now compare that with Captain Ahab in Herman Melville's *Moby Dick*. Ahab is physically surrounded by a crew, so he isn't isolated in the simple sense of being alone. But his obsession with hunting the white whale increasingly separates him emotionally and psychologically from the people around him. Ahab becomes less willing to listen to other perspectives. His private obsession dominates every decision he makes, and eventually he pulls the whole ship into his destructive pursuit. His isolation therefore has tragic consequences. It doesn't affect only Ahab; it contributes to disaster for nearly everyone around him. Jane Eyre provides another variation. Jane experiences isolation at several points in Charlotte Brontë's novel. As a child, she is excluded within her relatives' household, and later she spends long periods separated from people with whom she feels emotionally connected. But Jane doesn't respond to solitude in the same way as Frankenstein's creature or Ahab. At important moments, being alone gives her space to think through what she believes and what she wants. She develops independence and becomes more confident in making decisions based on her own moral judgment. So isolation is not automatically destructive in literature. It can expose vulnerability, intensify obsession, or encourage self knowledge, depending on the character and the circumstances. When we compare these characters, the useful question isn't simply, Is this person isolated? Instead, ask what caused the isolation, how the character responds to it, and what effect it has on the character's development and choices.
records.translation:
孤独出现在许多小说中，但作者可以以截然不同的方式运用它。
今天我想探讨一下，孤独是如何通过个体角色来体现的，以及它是如何塑造这些角色的。
让我们从玛丽·雪莱的《弗兰肯斯坦》开始。
这个怪物之所以被孤立，主要是因为他的外貌。
人们在了解他的个性之前，就因为恐惧而对他产生排斥。
他渴望陪伴，最初试图观察和理解人类社会，但反复的拒绝使他成为一个被排斥的人。
因此在这种情况下，孤独是由外部强加的。
他的外貌导致其他人排斥他。
现在，我们把它与赫尔曼·麦尔维尔的《白鲸》中的亚哈船长进行比较。
亚哈身体上被船员包围着，所以他并非简单意义上的独处。
但他对捕猎白鲸的执念，使他与周围的人在情感上和心理上日益疏远。
亚哈变得越来越不愿意听取其他观点。
他的私人执念主宰了他做出的每一个决定，最终他把整艘船都拖入了毁灭性的追逐中。
因此，他的孤独带来了悲剧性的后果。
它不仅影响了亚哈；它导致了几乎所有他周围的人的灾难。
《简·爱》提供了另一种变化。
简在夏洛特·勃朗特的小说中，多次经历孤独。
小时候，她在亲戚家被排斥，后来她长时间与那些她在情感上感到亲近的人分离。
但简对孤独的反应与弗兰肯斯坦的怪物或亚哈不同。
在关键时刻，独处给了她思考自己所信仰和渴望的空间。
她培养了独立性，并更加自信地根据自己的道德判断做出决定。
所以，孤独在文学中并非自动具有破坏性。
它可能暴露脆弱性，加剧执念，或鼓励自我认知，这取决于角色和具体情况。
当我们比较这些角色时，有用的问题不仅仅是，这个人是否被孤立了？
相反，要问是什么导致了孤独，角色如何回应它，以及它对角色的发展和选择有什么影响。

records.transcript: For your group assignment next week I've asked you to document your individual contributions. Some of you asked me why. The reason isn't only that I want to give everyone a fair grade, the main reason is actually rooted in psychology. In the late 1800s, a French agricultural engineer named Max Ringelman conducted a simple experiment. He asked people to pull on a rope, first alone, and then in groups. What he found was surprising. When people pulled in groups, the total force was less than the sum of individual efforts when pulling alone. In other words, people weren't pulling their weight when others were involved. This effect is called social loafing. Its existence was confirmed in later research in a study in the late 1970s. Researchers asked participants to cheer as loudly as they could, both alone and in groups. And individuals in groups made less noise per person than when cheering alone. But here's the good news. Social loafing often has a solution. In a study in the 1990s, participants were asked to brainstorm uses for a common object, like a brick, under two situations. In one situation, participants worked in groups, but were told their ideas would be individually identified and evaluated. In another situation, ideas were pooled anonymously. The results. When people knew their contributions would be linked to them personally, they generated higher quality responses. This shows that accountability and visibility can significantly decrease loafing. So basically, documenting your individual work for your upcoming group assignment will likely improve your overall project results.

原因不仅在于我想给每个人一个公平的评分，主要原因实际上根植于心理学。
在19世纪后期，一位名叫马克斯·林格尔曼的法国农业工程师进行了一个简单的实验。
他让人们拉绳子，先是独自一人，然后是分组进行。
他发现的结果令人惊讶。
当人们分组拉绳子时，总拉力小于个人独自拉绳子时的努力之和。
换句话说，当有其他人参与时，人们并没有尽全力。
这种效应被称为社会惰化。
它的存在在1970年代后期的一项研究中得到了证实。
研究人员要求参与者尽可能大声地欢呼，既有单独欢呼，也有分组欢呼。
结果是，分组欢呼时每个人发出的噪音比单独欢呼时要小。
但好消息是。
社会惰化通常有解决方案。
在1990年代的一项研究中，参与者被要求在两种情况下对常见物品（如砖块）的用途进行头脑风暴。
在一种情况下，参与者分组工作，但被告知他们的想法将单独识别和评估。
在另一种情况下，想法是匿名汇总的。
结果是。
当人们知道他们的贡献将与他们个人相关联时，他们会产生更高质量的回应。
这表明责任制和可见性可以显著减少惰化。
所以基本上，为即将到来的小组作业记录你的个人工作可能会提高你的整体项目成果。

transcriptSentences.text: For your group assignment next week I've asked you to document your individual contributions.
Some of you asked me why.
The reason isn't only that I want to give everyone a fair grade, the main reason is actually rooted in psychology.
In the late 1800s, a French agricultural engineer named Max Ringelman conducted a simple experiment.
He asked people to pull on a rope, first alone, and then in groups.
What he found was surprising.
When people pulled in groups, the total force was less than the sum of individual efforts when pulling alone.
In other words, people weren't pulling their weight when others were involved.
This effect is called social loafing.
Its existence was confirmed in later research in a study in the late 1970s.
Researchers asked participants to cheer as loudly as they could, both alone and in groups.
And individuals in groups made less noise per person than when cheering alone.
But here's the good news.
Social loafing often has a solution.
In a study in the 1990s, participants were asked to brainstorm uses for a common object, like a brick, under two situations.
In one situation, participants worked in groups, but were told their ideas would be individually identified and evaluated.
In another situation, ideas were pooled anonymously.
The results.
When people knew their contributions would be linked to them personally, they generated higher quality responses.
This shows that accountability and visibility can significantly decrease loafing.
So basically, documenting your individual work for your upcoming group assignment will likely improve your overall project results.

records.transcript: Some years ago, the government of Tanzania in Africa proposed building a 452 kilometer paved road in the north of the country, with the goal of boosting transportation and economic growth. The proposed route, though, would go through Serengeti National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and conservationists raised alarms. The road would bisect the annual migration corridor of wildebeests and other animals, potentially putting enormous pressure on their populations and disrupting the ecosystem in general. The models used by the conservationists showed that blocking the corridor with the road could reduce wildebeest populations by up to one third, disrupt predator prey dynamics and fragment an ecosystem that supports lions, cheetahs and countless other species. Increased traffic would also heighten poaching risks and introduce invasive species. The evidence wasn't conclusive, but because the risk was so serious and the consequences probably irreversible, the government decided to halt the project. That decision reflects what's known as the precautionary principle. When an action or policy poses a plausible risk of serious or irreversible harm, we shouldn't wait for absolute scientific certainty before deciding what to do. Why is this important? The consequences of indecision can be expensive or impossible to repair. Consider asbestos, once a widely used material for insulation and fireproofing. It was later linked to life threatening adverse effects on human health. But for decades, lack of consensus among researchers delayed government action, and by the time bans on asbestos were enacted, millions had been exposed, leading to costly litigation, cleanup and preventable deaths.

然而，拟议的路线将穿过塞伦盖蒂国家公园，一个联合国教科文组织世界遗产地，这引起了环保人士的警惕。
这条道路将横穿角马和其他动物的年度迁徙走廊，可能对其种群造成巨大压力，并总体上扰乱生态系统。

records.transcript: One of the most effective strategies in modern marketing is the use of storytelling. Storytelling involves crafting a narrative around a brand or product that engages consumers on an emotional level. Instead of simply listing features and benefits, marketers use stories to create a connection with their audience, making the brand memorable and relatable. This method has been especially powerful in the age of social media, where personal stories and viral content can significantly boost brand awareness and loyalty. Successful storytelling and marketing often includes elements like a compelling character, a relatable conflict, and a satisfying resolution. For example, a company selling eco friendly products might tell the story of a family striving to reduce their environmental footprint. This narrative not only highlights the product's benefits but also resonates with consumers who share similar values. Another aspect of storytelling and marketing is authenticity. Consumers are more likely to trust and engage with brands that appear genuine and transparent. This means that the story should reflect the brand's real values and mission, avoiding exaggeration or false claims. Visuals also play a crucial role in storytelling. High quality images and videos can bring the narrative to life, making it more impactful and easier to share. Of course, measuring the success of storytelling campaigns can be difficult, as traditional metrics like sales figures don't always capture the full impact of a well told story.

records.transcript: Today we're going to talk about cultural globalization. This is the process by which ideas, customs, entertainment, food, fashion, and other parts of culture move across national borders and become familiar to people in other parts of the world. One easy example is film. American movies are watched in countries all over the world, and viewers may become familiar with American styles of clothing, speech, food, or social behavior through those films. Of course, cultural exchange doesn't move in only one direction. Music from South Korea, films from India, and food traditions from many different regions have also gained international audiences. There are benefits to this kind of exchange. People can become more aware of ways of life that are different from their own, and artists can combine influences from several traditions. But cultural globalization can also create concerns. One of these is cultural appropriation. That's when people take an element from another culture, perhaps a style of clothing, a symbol, or a musical tradition, without understanding its meaning or treating the culture it came from with respect. Another concern is that widely distributed global products may make local cultures less visible. On the other hand, modern communication technology can work in the opposite direction too. Social media gives local musicians, artists, and communities a relatively easy way to share their culture with people around the world, even if they don't have the support of a large international company. So cultural globalization is not simply one culture replacing another. It's a complex process that can spread culture, create new combinations, and also raise questions about respect and cultural identity.

今天我们要讨论文化全球化。
这是思想、习俗、娱乐、食物、时尚以及其他文化元素跨越国界，并被世界其他地区的人们所熟知的过程。
一个简单的例子是电影。
美国的电影在世界各国都有播放，观众可以通过这些电影熟悉美国的服装风格、语言、食物或社交行为。
当然，文化交流并非单向的。
来自韩国的音乐、印度的电影以及许多不同地区的饮食传统也获得了国际受众。
这种交流有其益处。
人们可以更了解与自己不同的生活方式，艺术家也可以融合多种传统的影响。
但文化全球化也可能带来一些担忧。
其中之一是文化挪用。
这是指人们从另一种文化中获取一个元素，可能是服装风格、符号或音乐传统，但却不理解其含义，或不尊重其来源文化。
另一个担忧是，广泛传播的全球产品可能会使本地文化不那么显眼。

records.transcript: When you think of an animal flying over the ocean, a squid probably isn't the first thing that comes to mind. But several species of squid can actually leave the water and travel through the air for short distances. Flying squirrels don't truly fly. They climb to a high point and then glide downward using a membrane of skin between their legs. Flying squid are different because they can actually propel themselves upward from the water. Like other squid, they move underwater by taking water into their bodies and forcing it out through a tube called a siphon. When they approach the surface at high speed, that jet of water can launch them into the air. Once airborne, the squid spreads its fins and extends its arms and tentacles. Thin membranes between the arms and tentacles form a broad surface that functions somewhat like wings and helps stabilize the animal in the air. Some squid can travel many meters before returning to the water. Scientists aren't completely certain why squid do this. Escaping predators is one possible explanation. But researchers have also observed this behavior in groups of squid traveling together. Many flying squid make seasonal migrations, moving between different feeding and breeding areas at particular times of year. So their aerial behavior may be connected not only with avoiding predators but also with movement over long migration routes. Whatever the reason, it's a remarkable example of an animal using a form of movement we normally don't associate with life in the ocean.
records.translation:
当你想到一种在海洋上空飞行的动物时，鱿鱼可能不是你首先想到的。
但有几种鱿鱼实际上可以离开水面，在空中短距离飞行。
飞鼠并不是真正意义上的飞行。
它们爬到高处，然后利用腿之间的皮肤薄膜滑翔而下。
飞鱿鱼则不同，因为它们实际上可以从水中向上推进自己。
像其他鱿鱼一样，它们通过将水吸入体内并通过一个叫做虹吸管的管子将其喷出来在水下移动。
当它们高速接近水面时，那股水流可以将它们发射到空中。
一旦飞到空中，鱿鱼就会展开鱼鳍，伸展手臂和触手。
手臂和触手之间的薄膜形成一个宽阔的表面，其功能有点像翅膀，有助于稳定动物在空中的姿态。
有些鱿鱼能在空中移动许多米，然后才回到水中。
科学家们并不完全确定鱿鱼为什么会这样做。
逃避捕食者是一种可能的解释。
但研究人员也观察到成群结队的鱿鱼一起迁徙时有这种行为。
许多飞鱿鱼会进行季节性迁徙，在一年中的特定时间在不同的觅食区和繁殖区之间移动。
因此，它们的空中行为可能不仅与躲避捕食者有关，还与长距离迁徙路线上的移动有关。
无论原因如何，这都是一个了不起的例子，说明了一种动物使用我们通常不与海洋生物联系在一起的运动方式。

records.transcript: Most of us use LED lights every day, but the technology is important for much more than ordinary household lighting. LED stands for light emitting diode, and LEDs have changed the way light can be produced and used. One major advantage of LEDs is energy efficiency. Traditional incandescent bulbs create light by heating a thin wire until it becomes hot enough to glow. A large amount of the electrical energy is therefore lost as heat. LEDs produce light in a different way and require much less electricity to provide the same amount of illumination. They also last much longer, so they don't have to be replaced as often. Another important feature is their size. Individual LEDs can be extremely small. That gives designers much more flexibility than they have with traditional bulbs. LEDs can be arranged in thin displays, placed inside small electronic devices, or combined in large numbers to create lighting systems with very precise shapes and patterns. And researchers are still finding new applications. LEDs are already being used in automobile systems, medical equipment, indoor agriculture, and advanced display technologies. Future designs may allow lighting to respond more precisely to the environment or to be integrated into surfaces and devices in ways that are difficult to achieve today. So the importance of LEDs isn't limited to saving electricity. Their efficiency, small size, long life, and flexibility are continuing to open up new possibilities for how we use light.

records.transcript: Have you ever stared at a blank page, trying to come up with an idea of what to write about, waiting for inspiration? Storytelling dice are a simple way to break through that creative block. Yes, I'm talking about dice similar to ones you roll in some common board games to generate random numbers. But instead of numbers, each die is covered with pictorial symbols, like a tree, a key, or a lightning bolt. A typical set could have nine six sided dice. The magic lies in their unpredictability. You might roll a dragon, a locked door, and a storm. Suddenly, you're weaving a tale of, say, hidden realms and daring escapes. Storytelling dice are not just for writers. They can also serve as icebreakers at social gatherings. Imagine this. The party feels a little stiff, so you pull out the dice and say, Everyone roll three. Someone gets a dragon, a ladder, and a smiley face. Another rolls a spaceship, shoes, and a storm cloud. Soon, people are laughing as they connect these random images into a wild story. The dragon was stuck on a ladder during a thunderstorm. And then a spaceship landed to rescue it. It's silly, spontaneous, and gets everyone talking. But now, let's get back to creative writing and talk about a short story that a previous student of mine wrote last semester. While reading the story, try to guess what three images she rolled on her dice that inspired her to write it.

records.transcript: Back in 1938, a chemist named Roy Plunkett was working to create a new refrigerant, a new cooling substance. Plunkett was looking for an industrial refrigerant to replace the ones that existed at the time, which were toxic and flammable. Some, for example, could cause fatal poisoning if leaked. He was working with a gas called tetrafluoroethylene, or TFE, a highly flammable refrigerant. Plunkett stored TFE gas in cylinders, but one day he noticed that a cylinder of TFE no longer had gas in it. What was there? Well, powder, a solid. The TFE gas had solidified into this new powdery substance, polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. What made PTFE remarkable was its almost unprecedented stability, its resistance to heat, chemicals, and friction. It didn't react with other substances, making it ideal for industrial applications, like parts used in the aerospace industry, also medical devices and electronics. Eventually, PTFE began to be used in consumer products. Ever heard of Teflon, the nonstick coating on frying pans? That is PTFE, and it was used in homes around the world for many years. These days, you may be more likely to use stainless steel or cast iron cookware due to concerns with PTFE. Nevertheless, this is a classic example of serendipity in science. Plunkett wasn't trying to invent a nonstick surface. He stumbled upon it. This kind of discovery isn't rare. Scientists discovered X rays, penicillin, and many other scientific and medical innovations while trying to do something else.
records.translation:
回到1938年，一位名叫罗伊·普朗克特的化学家正在致力于研制一种新型制冷剂，一种新型冷却物质。
普朗克特正在寻找一种工业制冷剂来取代当时已有的那些有毒且易燃的制冷剂。
例如，有些制冷剂如果泄漏，可能会导致致命中毒。
他当时正在研究一种叫做四氟乙烯，或TFE的气体，这是一种高度易燃的制冷剂。
普朗克特把TFE气体储存在钢瓶里，但有一天他发现一个TFE钢瓶里没有气体了。
那里有什么呢？
嗯，是粉末，一种固体。
TFE气体凝固成了这种新的粉状物质，聚四氟乙烯，或PTFE。
PTFE之所以引人注目，是因为它几乎前所未有的稳定性，它耐热、耐化学品、耐摩擦。
它不与其他物质发生反应，这使得它非常适合工业应用，比如航空航天工业中使用的零件，还有医疗设备和电子产品。
最终，PTFE开始用于消费品。
听说过特氟龙吗？就是煎锅上的不粘涂层。
那就是PTFE，它在全球各地的家庭中使用了多年。
如今，由于对PTFE的担忧，你可能更倾向于使用不锈钢或铸铁炊具。
然而，这是科学中偶然发现的经典例子。
普朗克特并不是想发明一种不粘表面。
他是偶然发现的。
这种发现并不少见。
科学家在尝试做其他事情时，发现了X射线、青霉素以及许多其他科学和医学创新。

transcriptSentences.text: Back in 1938, a chemist named Roy Plunkett was working to create a new refrigerant, a new cooling substance.
Plunkett was looking for an industrial refrigerant to replace the ones that existed at the time, which were toxic and flammable.
Some, for example, could cause fatal poisoning if leaked.
He was working with a gas called tetrafluoroethylene, or TFE, a highly flammable refrigerant.
Plunkett stored TFE gas in cylinders, but one day he noticed that a cylinder of TFE no longer had gas in it.
What was there?
Well, powder, a solid.
The TFE gas had solidified into this new powdery substance, polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE.
What made PTFE remarkable was its almost unprecedented stability, its resistance to heat, chemicals, and friction.
It didn't react with other substances, making it ideal for industrial applications, like parts used in the aerospace industry, also medical devices and electronics.
Eventually, PTFE began to be used in consumer products.
Ever heard of Teflon, the nonstick coating on frying pans?
That is PTFE, and it was used in homes around the world for many years.
These days, you may be more likely to use stainless steel or cast iron cookware due to concerns with PTFE.
Nevertheless, this is a classic example of serendipity in science.
Plunkett wasn't trying to invent a nonstick surface.
He stumbled upon it.
This kind of discovery isn't rare.
Scientists discovered X rays, penicillin, and many other scientific and medical innovations while trying to do something else.

records.transcript: You've probably used many remote controls for things like televisions, smart devices, and other electronics. My wife uses one to open the gate to her parking lot at work. Now remote controls for TVs have been around since the 1950s. Wired remote controls had been used before then, back to around 1870, mostly for unpiloted military vehicles. Later, the inventor Nikola Tesla developed a wireless remote control for military vehicles in 1898. As for TV remotes, the first really popular one was developed in 1950. It was called the Lazy Bones and was pretty expensive. Fortunately, the Lazy Bones was connected to the TV by a long wire, which of course was annoying and a trip hazard. It's kind of hard to imagine this was more practical for most people than just getting up and turning the dial on the television yourself. A few years later, in 1955, a wireless remote was introduced, the Flashmatic. To use the Flashmatic, you'd point it at one of the corners of your TV screen. This would shine a light beam at the chosen corner. Now each corner had its own purpose, channel up or down, power or mute. Each corner had a photoelectric cell to convert the light beam into an electrical signal to do what you want. Trouble was, the photoelectric cells responded to other light sources too, like from a lightbulb or even sunlight. Imagine turning on a lightbulb and your TV suddenly turns on too.

records.transcript: Let's talk about lean manufacturing and its impact on efficiency in production processes. Lean manufacturing is a systematic approach to minimizing waste within a manufacturing system while maximizing productivity. While the methodology has been adopted by many companies worldwide, it was developed by a Japanese carmaker in the mid 20th century. But its roots can actually be traced to the supermarket. In the 1950s, Japanese engineers observed that supermarkets in the United States only restocked items as customers purchased them, maintaining just enough inventory to meet demand. This idea of just in time inventory management became a core principle of lean manufacturing. By identifying and removing excess inventory and eliminating other inefficiencies, companies could reduce costs and increase their overall productivity. Another important aspect of lean manufacturing is continuous improvement, often referred to as kai zhen. This involves constantly seeking ways to enhance processes, products and services. Companies at all levels are encouraged to contribute ideas for improvement, fostering a culture of innovation and teamwork. Lean manufacturing also emphasizes the importance of value from the customer's perspective. Companies focus on producing goods that meet customer needs and expectations, ensuring that each step in the production process adds value rather than unnecessary complexity. As you might imagine, implementing lean manufacturing requires a shift in organizational culture. Resistance to change and difficulty in sustaining improvements can get in the way. That said, companies that successfully adopt lean practices experience increased efficiency, reduced costs and higher customer satisfaction.
records.translation:
我们来谈谈精益生产及其对生产过程效率的影响。
精益生产是一种系统化的方法，旨在最大限度地减少制造系统中的浪费，同时最大限度地提高生产力。
尽管该方法已被全球许多公司采用，但它是在20世纪中叶由一家日本汽车制造商开发的。
但它的根源实际上可以追溯到超市。
在20世纪50年代，日本工程师观察到美国超市只在顾客购买商品后才补货，只维持足够的库存以满足需求。
这种即时库存管理理念成为精益生产的核心原则。
通过识别并消除过剩库存，以及消除其他低效率，公司可以降低成本并提高其整体生产力。
精益生产的另一个重要方面是持续改进，通常被称为“改善”。
这包括不断寻找方法来改进流程、产品和服务。
鼓励各级员工贡献改进意见，培养创新和团队合作的文化。

正如你可能想象的，实施精益生产需要组织文化的转变。
对变革的抵制以及难以持续改进可能会阻碍其发展。
尽管如此，成功采用精益实践的公司会体验到效率的提高、成本的降低和客户满意度的提升。

records.transcript: Some animals have such odd features and habits that they almost seem mythical. One is the Indian pangolin. The Indian pangolin is a mammal about 100 centimeters long. It has a tail, and except for its belly, it's covered in large, overlapping scales that make it look kind of like an artichoke or a pine cone. These scales are like its own coat of armor. When it's threatened, the Indian pangolin curls into a tight ball, protecting its belly and using its scales as a shield against predators. This behavior is known as volvation. Think of a hedgehog. When threatened, a hedgehog will also curl into a ball, volvation, with its spikes facing outward for protection. Ingenious. The Indian pangolin is found in forests, grasslands, and even deserts. Wherever Indian pangolins are, there are two things they like: digging and ants. Pangolins are nocturnal, meaning they come out at night. And when they do, they're looking for ants. They eat about 200,000 of them, ants and termites, every day. This helps keep their ecosystem balanced. They also dig burrows, which are holes or tunnels, to sleep in, hide in, or raise their young. As they dig, they disturb and loosen the soil. That action mixes nutrients, lets air and water move through the ground more easily, and makes the soil healthier for plants to grow in.

records.transcript: Today, we're discussing the concept of dark stores. That is, retail centers that resemble warehouses and are usually located near city centers. Unlike traditional storefronts, they are not designed for walk in customers, but function as fulfillment hubs optimized for rapid online delivery. The rise of dark stores has been fueled by the growing demand for online shopping, especially in urban areas where space is limited and rent is high. The main appeal of dark stores lies in their efficiency. By eliminating the traditional storefront, businesses can reduce overhead costs and pass savings on to consumers through lower prices. Their proximity to dense urban areas also allows for faster delivery times, meeting the expectations of customers who value speed and convenience. For instance, a company might deliver groceries in under an hour, giving it a major competitive advantage over traditional supermarkets. However, dark stores are not without drawbacks. Their expansion can contribute to the decline of traditional retail spaces, creating economic challenges for local businesses. Employment is another concern. While these centers generate jobs in logistics and delivery, they may reduce the number of customer facing roles available in physical stores. Looking ahead, many experts predict that dark stores will continue to reshape the retail landscape. Some may adopt advanced automation, further reducing the need for human labor and potentially redefining the shopping experience itself. As with other technological shifts, the key challenge will be balancing efficiency with the broader social and economic implications of these changes.

今天，我们来讨论“暗店”的概念。
也就是说，它们是类似仓库的零售中心，通常位于市中心附近。
与传统店面不同，它们不是为顾客上门购物而设计的，而是作为履约中心，专为快速在线配送而优化。
暗店的兴起得益于在线购物需求的增长，尤其是在空间有限、租金高昂的城市地区。
暗店的主要吸引力在于其效率。
通过取消传统店面，企业可以降低运营成本，并通过更低的价格将节省的开支转嫁给消费者。
它们靠近人口稠密的城市地区，也使得配送时间更快，满足了重视速度和便利性的客户的期望。
例如，一家公司可以在一小时内配送杂货，这使其比传统超市具有显著的竞争优势。
然而，暗店并非没有缺点。
它们的扩张可能导致传统零售空间的衰落，给当地企业带来经济挑战。
就业是另一个问题。
虽然这些中心在物流和配送方面创造了就业机会，但它们可能会减少实体店中面向客户的职位数量。
展望未来，许多专家预测暗店将继续重塑零售格局。
有些可能会采用先进的自动化技术，进一步减少对人力的需求，并可能重新定义购物体验本身。
与其他技术变革一样，主要挑战将是在效率与这些变革更广泛的社会和经济影响之间取得平衡。

records.transcript: Have you ever thought about how ancient concrete structures, like Roman amphitheaters and aqueducts, have managed to last for thousands of years, while modern concrete buildings seem to fall apart and need replacing after just a few decades? For a long time, researchers thought the secret to Roman concrete's durability was volcanic ash. That makes sense, since volcanic ash was a major ingredient, and it was explicitly described as such by architects and historians who were writing at the time. But it turns out the real secret was actually tiny chunks of calcium carbonate. These formed because the Romans used dry quicklime in their mix, instead of the way we make concrete today, called Portland cement, where lime gets mixed with water first, then the concrete is then blended with everything else. When cracks show up in Roman concrete and water gets in, those calcium carbonate bits react with the water and seal up the cracks. So, the concrete basically heals itself, fixes the cracks, and gets stronger over time. Funny thing is, researchers have noticed these chunks in Roman concrete for ages, but they just figured they were a production flaw, like someone didn't mix the ingredients well at all. Anyway, considering how short lived modern concrete is, and the fact that making it is bad for the environment, it's pretty exciting to think we might be able to use some of these ancient Roman tricks in future construction.
records.translation:
你有没有想过，古老的混凝土结构，比如罗马圆形剧场和高架渠，是如何历经千年而不倒的，而现代的混凝土建筑却似乎在几十年后就支离破碎、需要更换了呢？
很长一段时间以来，研究人员认为罗马混凝土耐用的秘密是火山灰。
这很合理，因为火山灰是主要成分，而且当时的建筑师和历史学家也明确记载了这一点。
但事实证明，真正的秘密其实是微小的碳酸钙块。
这些块状物之所以形成，是因为罗马人在混合物中使用了干生石灰，而不是我们今天制作混凝土的方式，即所谓的波特兰水泥，波特兰水泥是石灰先与水混合，然后再将混凝土与所有其他材料混合。
当罗马混凝土出现裂缝并渗入水时，这些碳酸钙颗粒会与水发生反应并封闭裂缝。
所以，混凝土基本上可以自我修复，修补裂缝，并随着时间的推移变得更坚固。
有趣的是，研究人员很早就注意到了罗马混凝土中的这些块状物，但他们只是认为那是一个生产缺陷，就像有人根本没有把配料混合好一样。
总之，考虑到现代混凝土的寿命如此之短，以及制造它对环境有害的事实，我们也许能够将这些古罗马的技巧运用到未来的建筑中，这真是令人兴奋。

transcriptSentences.text: Have you ever thought about how ancient concrete structures, like Roman amphitheaters and aqueducts, have managed to last for thousands of years, while modern concrete buildings seem to fall apart and need replacing after just a few decades?
For a long time, researchers thought the secret to Roman concrete's durability was volcanic ash.
That makes sense, since volcanic ash was a major ingredient, and it was explicitly described as such by architects and historians who were writing at the time.
But it turns out the real secret was actually tiny chunks of calcium carbonate.

These formed because the Romans used dry quicklime in their mix, instead of the way we make concrete today, called Portland cement, where lime gets mixed with water first, then the concrete is then blended with everything else.
When cracks show up in Roman concrete and water gets in, those calcium carbonate bits react with the water and seal up the cracks.
So, the concrete basically heals itself, fixes the cracks, and gets stronger over time.
Funny thing is, researchers have noticed these chunks in Roman concrete for ages, but they just figured they were a production flaw, like someone didn't mix the ingredients well at all.

Anyway, considering how short lived modern concrete is, and the fact that making it is bad for the environment, it's pretty exciting to think we might be able to use some of these ancient Roman tricks in future construction.

records.transcript: Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available. Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and converts it to electricity or heat. The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them. The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero harmful pollutants. Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels. But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Another advantage, and one we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas, far from the grid. So what are the disadvantages? Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which of course reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels. That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non sunny periods. Panel lifespan is quite good at 25 to 30 years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that, so waste is increasing faster than expected. This is a problem because recycling them is expensive, and most panels end up in landfills.

让我们在可再生能源系列中继续讨论太阳能，这可以说是最丰富的可用资源。

这项技术主要采用太阳能电池板，由光伏电池组成，当阳光照射时，这些电池会产生电流。
太阳能的优点众所周知，最重要的一点可能是它不产生有害污染物。
任何工业活动都会以这样或那样的方式产生二氧化碳，而制造太阳能电池板本身就需要化石燃料提供的能源。

records.transcript: Before we begin, here's a little background. Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian artist and inventor who lived during the Renaissance, a period of renewed interest in science, art, and human knowledge. He is best known for paintings such as the Mona Lisa, but he also studied anatomy, engineering, and mechanics, often combining these interests in his work. And today, we'll talk about one of his lesser known works, his design of a robot. In 1495, Leonardo designed what we now call Leonardo's Robot, or the Mechanical Knight. So, to be clear, this was long before the term robot entered our vocabulary. Leonardo was fascinated with human anatomy, not really surprising for a painter. And this fascination directly influenced his robotic design, a synthesis of his varied interests. Leonardo sketched an intricate, human like robot that would mimic human actions. The knight was meant to be wearing armour, and was designed to move its arms, raise its visor, and even hug a person. This knight might not have been built during Leonardo's lifetime, but the designs highlight mechanical understanding that was remarkable for the period. They reveal an in depth understanding of gears, pulleys, principles of weight distribution. These sketches made by Leonardo were actually rediscovered in the 1950s by a Leonardo scholar. This scholar studied these sketches, but it wasn't until 2002 that the most complete physical reconstruction of the robot was made. This robot was able to walk and wave, an incredible feat considering how long ago Leonardo created his sketches.
records.translation:
在我们开始之前，先来了解一下背景知识。
列奥纳多·达·芬奇是一位意大利艺术家和发明家，生活在文艺复兴时期，这是一个对科学、艺术和人类知识重新产生兴趣的时期。
他以《蒙娜丽莎》等画作而闻名，但他也研究解剖学、工程学和力学，并经常将这些兴趣融入到他的作品中。
今天，我们将讨论他鲜为人知的一项作品，他的机器人设计。
1495年，列奥纳多设计了我们现在称之为列奥纳多机器人，或称机械骑士的东西。
所以，要明确的是，这比“机器人”这个词进入我们的词汇要早得多。
列奥纳多对人体解剖学着迷，这对于一位画家来说并不奇怪。
这种着迷直接影响了他的机器人设计，这是他各种兴趣的综合体现。
列奥纳多画了一个复杂的、像人一样的机器人，它能模仿人类的动作。
这个骑士应该穿着盔甲，设计成可以移动手臂、抬起面罩，甚至拥抱一个人。
这个骑士可能在列奥纳多的有生之年没有被建造出来，但这些设计突出了那个时代非凡的机械理解。
它们揭示了对齿轮、滑轮、重量分布原理的深入理解。
列奥纳多绘制的这些草图实际上是在20世纪50年代被一位列奥纳多学者重新发现的。
这位学者研究了这些草图，但直到2002年才完成了机器人最完整的物理重建。
这个机器人能够行走和挥手，考虑到列奥纳多创作这些草图的年代久远，这是一项令人难以置信的壮举。

records.transcript: Ever wonder why some rewards motivate better than others when you're trying to change behavior? Most people think of rewards as tangible things: money, candy, gift cards. These are what psychologists call extrinsic rewards because they come from an external source. But in the 1960s, psychologist David Premack had a different idea. Instead of giving people tangible things, why not use activities people already enjoy? This became Premack's principle. Here are the basics. You can use something someone already likes to do, or a high probability behavior, to motivate an activity they avoid, or a low probability behavior. Here's an example. If a child loves playing outside but hates cleaning their room, you make outdoor play the reward for cleaning. First clean, then play. It's simple but powerful. Premack believed this strategy works better than candy or money because it motivates by tapping into what psychologists call intrinsic rewards, things that feel good because we genuinely enjoy them. Tangible rewards often lose their appeal, but favorite activities stay motivating. By linking something less appealing to something naturally fun, you create a lasting incentive that feels personal and meaningful. Think about it. If you're trying to get yourself to the gym more often, you might promise yourself extra time on a hobby you love after your workout. You're not bribing yourself with something artificial or external. You're connecting the new habit to something that already matters to you. That's why Premack's principle is still relevant today and not just for parents and teachers.

records.transcript: Earlier in class, we talked about the Dutch tulip craze of the early 1600s, a time when tulip bulbs became luxury symbols, prices soared, and fortunes vanished almost overnight. It was one of history's first economic bubbles, fueled by speculation and status. America had its own version in the early 19th century, when the country was swept up in the mulberry craze. The idea sounded simple. Plant mulberry trees, raise the silkworms that eat their leaves, collect the silk from the worms' cocoons, and rake in the profits. Silk was a prized luxury import, and producing it locally promised enormous wealth. Farmers and investors rushed to buy mulberry saplings. Prices for the young trees soared from pennies to several dollars. Classic bubble behavior. And the speculation wasn't all about money. Silk itself, the idea of silk, carried powerful symbolism. Refinement, status, and aspiration. For a brief moment, middle class Americans imagined silk dresses as attainable, blurring old class distinctions. But reality intervened. Silkworms are delicate, requiring precise care and stable climates. Harsh winters wiped out silkworm populations across the country. Mulberry groves lost their purpose. The trees lost their value. The bubble burst, and by the mid 1840s, folks who'd invested their fortunes in the venture were ruined financially. And the bottom line? I mean, for us today? Well, just like tulip mania in the Netherlands, the American mulberry craze shows how ambition and hype can outpace ecological and practical limits. This is a cautionary tale for modern day investment booms.

records.transcript: Why do some companies thrive, while others with similar resources falter? Organizational agility might hold the key. Organizational agility is a company's ability to quickly adapt to market changes, by making fast decisions, being flexible and responsive to customer needs, and being able to reconfigure internal structures when needed. Take an example you're probably familiar with, a streaming media company that began as a DVD rental service. It successfully pivoted to online streaming, just as internet speeds improved, and later moved into producing original content. These shifts were strategic and fast. They allowed the company to stay ahead of consumer expectations and industry trends. Agility also means responding to customer demands. A well known clothing retailer, for instance, designed its supply chain to move new styles from concept to store in just a few weeks. If a celebrity wears a bold new look, this retailer can have a similar item on shelves, while competitors are still in the design phase. That kind of responsiveness keeps the brand alive. Agility is a key. It's a key to keep the brand relevant. Agility comes with hurdles, like cultural resistance. In one case, a large industrial firm tried to adopt agile practices across its divisions. This meant forming cross functional teams, groups made up of people from different departments, like engineering, marketing, and operations, who would collaborate on shared goals. But many employees had spent decades in the industry, spent decades in rigid hierarchies, with clearly defined roles. Cross functional teams felt chaotic and unfamiliar. This industrial firm had to invest in training to help employees understand that agility wasn't about abandoning structure, but about building smarter, more responsive systems.
records.translation:
为什么有些公司能蓬勃发展，而另一些拥有相似资源的公司却步履维艰？
组织敏捷性可能就是关键。
组织敏捷性是指公司通过快速决策、灵活响应客户需求以及在需要时重新配置内部结构，来快速适应市场变化的能力。

这些转变是战略性的，而且速度很快。
它们让公司能够超越消费者预期，引领行业趋势。
敏捷性也意味着响应客户需求。
例如，一家知名的服装零售商设计其供应链，能够在几周内将新款式从概念变为门店商品。
如果某位名人穿上大胆的新款，这家零售商就能在竞争对手仍处于设计阶段时，将类似商品摆上货架。

records.transcript: The Western Roman Empire, which flourished for about the first five centuries of the first millennium, is often celebrated for its engineering marvels. But one of its lesser known achievements is its contribution to urban planning. Roman towns were laid out with remarkable precision, often following a grid system which was quite advanced for its time. Streets intersected at right angles, dividing the city into organized blocks that made navigation easier and promoted efficient trade, communication, and administration. At the heart of every Roman city was the forum, a multifunctional space that served as the civic, commercial, and social hub. It was the heart of public life, where citizens gathered for various activities ranging from political discussions to socializing. Surrounding it were carefully zoned areas, residential quarters, marketplaces, temples, and public buildings, each with a designated place in the urban fabric. This early form of zoning helped maintain order and efficiency. Romans also prioritized infrastructure. Roads were paved and well drained, and public amenities like baths, latrines, and fountains were strategically placed to serve dense populations. Their cities were designed not just for grandeur but for functionality, though that balance wasn't always perfect. In poorer districts, overcrowded housing led to sanitation problems and fire hazards, revealing the limits of even the most advanced planning. Still, Roman urban design laid the groundwork for modern city planning. Concepts like grid layouts, centralized public spaces, and functional zoning trace their roots to these ancient innovations. The legacy of Roman urbanism lives on in many cities today.

罗马城镇的布局非常精确，常常遵循网格系统，这在当时是相当先进的。
街道以直角相交，将城市划分成有组织的街区，使导航更容易，并促进了高效的贸易、通讯和管理。

它是公共生活的中心，市民们在那里进行各种活动，从政治讨论到社交。
围绕着广场的是精心划定的区域，包括居民区、市场、寺庙和公共建筑，每个在城市结构中都有其指定的位置。

records.transcript: One of the most fascinating aspects of human culture is gift giving. While it might seem simple, it's actually a deeply social act shaped by cultural norms. Anthropologists have found that gifts aren't just about exchanging goods, they're about building relationships. In many indigenous communities, gift giving plays a central role in ceremonies and rituals. For example, in the potlatch tradition among indigenous groups in the Pacific Northwest, gifts like food, blankets, or tools are exchanged during communal gatherings to honor guests, mark life events, and reinforce social bonds. These gifts carry meaning and create mutual obligations, helping maintain harmony and unity within the group. Now, interestingly, receiving a gift often comes with an expectation to give back, not immediately, but eventually. Anthropologist Marcel Mauss described this as a spirit of reciprocity. And what's important is that it's not just a one time transaction of you gave me something, so I'll give you something. This cycle is often repeated in a continuous loop, creating long term connections and trust. Over time, this rhythm of giving and returning strengthens relationships and community ties. Okay, now in more formal settings, like business and diplomacy, gift giving can signal goodwill, but cultural sensitivity is key. For instance, while a potted plant might seem thoughtful and eco friendly, in some cultures it could symbolize something negative, making it unsuitable for formal occasions. So knowing what's appropriate really matters.
records.translation:
人类文化中最引人入胜的方面之一就是送礼。
虽然这看起来很简单，但它实际上是一种深受文化规范影响的深刻的社会行为。
人类学家发现，送礼不仅仅是为了交换物品，更是为了建立人际关系。
在许多原住民社区中，送礼在仪式和典礼中扮演着核心角色。
例如，在太平洋西北地区原住民群体的散财宴传统中，食物、毯子或工具等礼物在公共聚会期间进行交换，以尊敬客人、纪念人生事件并加强社会联系。
这些礼物承载着意义并产生相互义务，有助于维持群体内部的和睦与团结。
现在，有趣的是，收到礼物往往伴随着回赠的期望，不是立即，而是最终。
人类学家马塞尔·莫斯将其描述为一种互惠精神。
重要的是，这不仅仅是一次性的交易，即你给了我东西，所以我也给你东西。
这个循环经常在持续的循环中重复，从而建立长期的联系和信任。
随着时间的推移，这种给予和回馈的节奏加强了人际关系和社区联系。
好的，现在在更正式的场合，如商业和外交中，送礼可以表示善意，但文化敏感性是关键。
例如，盆栽植物可能看起来周到且环保，但在某些文化中，它可能象征负面事物，使其不适合正式场合。
因此，了解什么是合适的确实很重要。

transcriptSentences.text: One of the most fascinating aspects of human culture is gift giving.
While it might seem simple, it's actually a deeply social act shaped by cultural norms.
Anthropologists have found that gifts aren't just about exchanging goods, they're about building relationships.
In many indigenous communities, gift giving plays a central role in ceremonies and rituals.

For example, in the potlatch tradition among indigenous groups in the Pacific Northwest, gifts like food, blankets, or tools are exchanged during communal gatherings to honor guests, mark life events, and reinforce social bonds.
These gifts carry meaning and create mutual obligations, helping maintain harmony and unity within the group.
Now, interestingly, receiving a gift often comes with an expectation to give back, not immediately, but eventually.
Anthropologist Marcel Mauss described this as a spirit of reciprocity.
And what's important is that it's not just a one time transaction of you gave me something, so I'll give you something.
This cycle is often repeated in a continuous loop, creating long term connections and trust.
Over time, this rhythm of giving and returning strengthens relationships and community ties.
Okay, now in more formal settings, like business and diplomacy, gift giving can signal goodwill, but cultural sensitivity is key.
For instance, while a potted plant might seem thoughtful and eco friendly, in some cultures it could symbolize something negative, making it unsuitable for formal occasions.
So knowing what's appropriate really matters.

records.transcript: During the early 20th century, technology was advancing rapidly, and music was undergoing a transformation of its own. Electrophones were at the forefront of this evolution. All right, so electrophones. They're the predecessors of today's synthesizers. And electrophones challenged established musical conventions. They create sound using electronic means, a groundbreaking innovation for their time. Take, for example, the theremin. The theremin is an instrument that lets you create melodies through the manipulation of electromagnetic fields. You don't even touch it. There's no direct physical contact with the instrument. The theremin made its mark on the landscape of music, and its tones became synonymous with experimental compositions. Similarly, the Ondes Martenot gave musicians a new and expressive range of sounds. You play it by gliding a ring along a wire, kind of like how you move a bow across the strings of a violin. These electrophones, the theremin and the Ondes Martenot, set the stage for the synthesizers that dominate today's music. Electrophones enabled composers of the early 20th century to explore new musical ideas. Despite being overshadowed by modern electronics, these early electrophones made an important and lasting mark on music. And they continue to influence music making. Artists are going to keep looking forward in their quest to redefine musical boundaries. But we can also look back to acknowledge the foundational role these early electrophones played in shaping the history of music.

records.transcript: Today we're discussing the concept of dark stores, retail centers that resemble warehouses and are usually located near city centers. Unlike traditional storefronts, they are not designed for walk in customers but function as fulfillment hubs optimized for rapid online delivery. The rise of dark stores has been fueled by the growing demand for online shopping, especially in urban areas where space is limited and rent is high. The main appeal of dark stores lies in their efficiency. By eliminating the traditional storefront, businesses can reduce overhead costs and pass the savings on to consumers through lower prices. Their proximity to dense urban areas also allows for faster delivery times, meeting the expectations of customers who value speed and convenience. For instance, a company might deliver groceries in under an hour, giving it a major competitive advantage over traditional supermarkets. However, dark stores are not without drawbacks. Their expansion can contribute to the decline of traditional retail spaces, creating economic challenges for local businesses. Employment is another concern. While these centers generate jobs in warehousing and delivery, they may reduce the number of customer facing roles available in physical stores. Looking ahead, many experts predict that dark stores will continue to reshape the retail landscape. Some may adopt advanced automation, further reducing the need for human labor and potentially redefining the shopping experience itself. As with other technological shifts, the key challenge will be balancing efficiency with the broader social and economic implications of these changes.

records.transcript: Today I've got a topic that might just electrify your imagination. Lightning in the atmosphere of Venus. You might wonder why we should care about lightning on another planet. Well, understanding lightning on Venus could give us clues about the planet's dynamic weather systems. Okay, so the Soviet Venera space missions set out to explore Venus, one of Earth's closest neighbors. What these missions found was surprising. Evidence of lightning in Venus's thick, sulfuric acid laden clouds. So picture this. The sky is perpetually cloaked in clouds. Lightning flickers through the gloom. It's practically the setting for a science fiction movie. But this isn't fiction; it's real science. And here's where it gets interesting: the presence of lightning suggests that the atmosphere of Venus is more dynamic than we once assumed. Why does this matter? Lightning can play a crucial role in atmospheric chemistry, affecting the formation of molecules and influencing weather patterns. On Earth, lightning is known to create compounds like nitrogen oxides, which are essential for plant life. While Venus doesn't have plant life, understanding its atmospheric processes helps scientists build models that can be applied to other planets, including our own. Moreover, studying Venusian lightning can help us predict future changes in its atmosphere. If lightning is as prevalent as the Venera missions suggest, it could mean that Venus is more geologically active than previously assumed. This suggests new ideas for research. Could other planets with similar conditions harbor surprising phenomena, or even forms of life?

records.transcript: One of the most fascinating aspects of human culture is gift giving. While it might seem simple, it's actually a deeply social act shaped by cultural norms. Anthropologists have found that gifts aren't just about exchanging goods; they're about building relationships. In many Indigenous communities, gift giving plays a central role in ceremonies and rituals. For example, in the potlatch tradition among Indigenous groups in the Pacific Northwest, gifts like food, blankets, or tools are exchanged during communal gatherings to honor guests, mark life events, and reinforce social bonds. These gifts carry meaning and create mutual obligations, helping maintain harmony and unity within the group. Now, interestingly, receiving a gift often comes with an expectation to give back, not immediately, but eventually. Anthropologist Marcel Mauss described this as a spirit of reciprocity. And what's important is that it's not just a one time transaction of you gave me something, so I'll give you something. This cycle is often repeated in a continuous loop, creating long term connections and trust. Over time, this rhythm of giving and returning strengthens relationships and community ties. Okay, now in more formal settings, like business and diplomacy, gift giving can signal goodwill, but cultural sensitivity is key. For instance, while a potted plant might seem thoughtful and eco friendly, in some cultures it could symbolize something negative, making it unsuitable for formal occasions. records.transcript: We've been talking about the iconic North American monarch butterflies. Many monarch butterflies migrate annually between the northern United States, where they spend summer, and Mexico, where they spend winter. Previously, however, researchers could only guess at some details of monarch butterfly migrations. They knew where the butterflies started and ended their journey, but not what happened in between. Now, with the help of new tracking devices, scientists can track precise routes, including stopover points and even detours. This level of detail could reveal how climate patterns and habitat loss affect migration success. Early data have already revealed surprises. For example, some monarch butterflies take far longer pauses than we ever imagined. Specifically, several butterflies that were tagged with the tracking devices in Kansas lingered for nearly two weeks in central Texas before continuing southward. These extended stopovers may help butterflies refuel and recover energy, reshaping how conservationists think about preserving habitats along the migration corridor. The technology isn't without challenges, however. The tracking devices depend on sunlight for power, so dense cloud cover along migration routes can limit data collection. Despite these and other hurdles, the knowledge gained could be vital for saving one of nature's most iconic creatures.

我们一直在谈论标志性的北美帝王蝶。
许多帝王蝶每年在它们度过夏季的美国北部和度过冬季的墨西哥之间迁徙。
然而，在此之前，研究人员只能猜测帝王蝶迁徙的一些细节。
他们知道蝴蝶的旅程始于何处，终于何处，但不知道中间发生了什么。
现在，在新追踪设备的帮助下，科学家可以追踪精确的路线，包括中途停留点甚至绕道。
这种详细程度可以揭示气候模式和栖息地丧失如何影响迁徙的成功。
早期数据已经揭示了一些惊喜。
例如，一些帝王蝶暂停的时间比我们想象的要长得多。
具体来说，在堪萨斯州被标记上追踪设备的几只蝴蝶在德克萨斯州中部停留了近两周，然后才继续南行。

追踪设备依靠阳光供电，因此迁徙路线上的浓密云层可能会限制数据收集。

records.transcript: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. One of its most recognizable features is its Great Red Spot, which is actually a huge storm. It appears as a large red oval on the planet's surface and has been observed for centuries. This storm is enormous, larger than the planet Earth, and it's been raging for centuries. But did you know that the Great Red Spot is actually shrinking? This topic is interesting not only for astronomers, but also for anyone who studies weather system dynamics, even though this exists on a much larger scale than we're used to for weather we experience on Earth. The shrinkage of the Great Red Spot could give us clues about Jupiter's atmosphere and maybe even our own. Jupiter's atmosphere is primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. It's the trace gases and cloud dynamics that make it fascinating. As the Great Red Spot shrinks, we study changes in wind patterns and atmospheric conditions, hoping for insights into the underlying processes. It could help us understand atmospheric evolution, not only on Jupiter, but potentially on Earth or other planets. Why is it shrinking? The exact reasons remain a mystery. Some theories suggest interactions with other atmospheric features, like smaller storms or jet streams, might be contributing factors. As we continue to observe and gather data, the Great Red Spot's changes could unlock secrets about weather patterns, atmospheric stability, and planetary evolution. So let's get to that: the data.

records.transcript: During the Roman Empire, soldiers had a lot of weapons and armor, and they needed a place to store them, their arms and armor. Soldiers used boxes called armariums to store this gear. Armariums were big portable wooden storage boxes. Later, people including civilians kept using armariums in their homes, but to store items like clothing, books, or other valuables. In France in the sixteenth century, wealthy people had them and called them armoires. Armoire is a term we still use today for a large standalone piece of wooden furniture for storing things. Around the same time, some homes in England started to have what they called closets. But these closets were more like small studies, where people could store things, or also just read or be alone. Someone might play their guitar in one to relax. So both the armoire and the English closet were kind of precursors to the modern closet. If we fast forward to the mid 1800s in the early United States, we're starting to see closets that are built directly into homes as part of the floor plan. The big benefit of these was that they were less pricey than armoires, way cheaper. People had less clothing then than they do today, and they'd usually use a small chest to store clothes or hang them on a peg or hook. Coat hangers weren't invented until the late 1800s, but still closets in the home were handy places to store other belongings.
records.translation:
在罗马帝国时期，士兵们有很多武器和盔甲，他们需要一个地方来存放这些装备，即他们的武器和盔甲。
士兵们使用叫做“armariums”的箱子来存放这些装备。
“Armariums”是大型便携式木制储物箱。
后来，包括平民在内的人们继续在家里使用“armariums”，但用来存放衣物、书籍或其他贵重物品。
在16世纪的法国，富人拥有它们并称之为“armoires”。
“Armoire”是我们今天仍然使用的一个术语，指一种大型独立式木制家具，用于存放物品。
大约在同一时期，英国的一些家庭开始拥有他们称之为“closets”的东西。
但这些“closets”更像小书房，人们可以在里面存放东西，也可以只是阅读或独处。
有人可能会在里面弹吉他放松一下。
所以，“armoire”和英式“closet”都算是现代壁橱的前身。
如果我们将时间快进到19世纪中叶的早期美国，我们开始看到直接作为房屋平面图一部分建造的壁橱。
这些壁橱的最大好处是它们比“armoires”便宜得多，价格实惠得多。
当时人们的衣服比现在少，他们通常会用一个小箱子来存放衣服，或者把它们挂在挂钩或钉子上。
衣架直到19世纪末才被发明出来，但家里的壁橱仍然是存放其他物品的便利场所。

transcriptSentences.text: During the Roman Empire, soldiers had a lot of weapons and armor, and they needed a place to store them, their arms and armor.
Soldiers used boxes called armariums to store this gear.
Armariums were big portable wooden storage boxes.
Later, people including civilians kept using armariums in their homes, but to store items like clothing, books, or other valuables.
In France in the sixteenth century, wealthy people had them and called them armoires.
Armoire is a term we still use today for a large standalone piece of wooden furniture for storing things.
Around the same time, some homes in England started to have what they called closets.
But these closets were more like small studies, where people could store things, or also just read or be alone.
Someone might play their guitar in one to relax.
So both the armoire and the English closet were kind of precursors to the modern closet.
If we fast forward to the mid 1800s in the early United States, we're starting to see closets that are built directly into homes as part of the floor plan.
The big benefit of these was that they were less pricey than armoires, way cheaper.
People had less clothing then than they do today, and they'd usually use a small chest to store clothes or hang them on a peg or hook.
Coat hangers weren't invented until the late 1800s, but still closets in the home were handy places to store other belongings.

records.transcript: How did you wake up this morning? You probably had some kind of alarm. Well, what did people do long ago in ancient Greece, when people relied on natural indicators like the sun's position for time? One clever solution was the clepsydra, a water clock. This was essentially a container filled with water that drained at a steady rate. The dropping water level marked the passage of time and at a certain point, it triggered a mechanism to produce sound, effectively serving as an alarm clock. Ingenious, right? Fast forward to the late nineteenth century when the industrial age came into full swing. The need for punctuality in factories led to the development of wind up mechanical alarm clocks. These devices, with their recognizable bells, were widely used until the twentieth century brought about a significant change, the electric alarm clock. By eliminating the need to wind the clock, these electric models revolutionized how people manage their mornings, offering convenience and accuracy like never before. In the late twentieth century, digital technology further transformed our alarm clocks with LED displays and snooze buttons, adding more layers of utility. These devices serve an important function, and our relationship with alarm clocks also reflects cultural evolution. Clocks transition from simple time keepers to indispensable companions in our daily routines, influencing how we perceive time management and punctuality. And if you really want to talk about an indispensable companion in our daily routine, you might have one in your pocket, the mobile phone.
records.translation:
你今天早上是怎么醒来的？
你可能用了某种闹钟。
那么，很久以前在古希腊，当人们依靠太阳位置等自然指标来计时时，他们是怎么做的呢？
一个巧妙的解决方案是水钟，即漏壶。
这本质上是一个装满水的容器，水以稳定的速度流出。
下降的水位标志着时间的流逝，在某个特定点，它会触发一个机制发出声音，有效地充当闹钟。
很巧妙，对吧？
快进到十九世纪后期，工业时代全面兴起。
工厂对准时的需求导致了发条机械闹钟的发展。
这些带有可识别铃声的设备被广泛使用，直到二十世纪带来了重大变革，即电动闹钟。
通过消除上发条的需要，这些电动模型彻底改变了人们管理早晨的方式，提供了前所未有的便利和准确性。
在二十世纪后期，数字技术通过LED显示屏和贪睡按钮进一步改变了我们的闹钟，增加了更多的实用性。
这些设备具有重要的功能，我们与闹钟的关系也反映了文化演变。
时钟从简单的计时器转变为我们日常生活中不可或缺的伴侣，影响着我们对时间管理和守时的看法。
如果你真的想谈论我们日常生活中不可或缺的伴侣，你可能口袋里就有一个，那就是手机。

transcriptSentences.text: How did you wake up this morning?
You probably had some kind of alarm.
Well, what did people do long ago in ancient Greece, when people relied on natural indicators like the sun's position for time?
One clever solution was the clepsydra, a water clock.
This was essentially a container filled with water that drained at a steady rate.
The dropping water level marked the passage of time and at a certain point, it triggered a mechanism to produce sound, effectively serving as an alarm clock.
Ingenious, right?
Fast forward to the late nineteenth century when the industrial age came into full swing.
The need for punctuality in factories led to the development of wind up mechanical alarm clocks.
These devices, with their recognizable bells, were widely used until the twentieth century brought about a significant change, the electric alarm clock.
By eliminating the need to wind the clock, these electric models revolutionized how people manage their mornings, offering convenience and accuracy like never before.
In the late twentieth century, digital technology further transformed our alarm clocks with LED displays and snooze buttons, adding more layers of utility.
These devices serve an important function, and our relationship with alarm clocks also reflects cultural evolution.
Clocks transition from simple time keepers to indispensable companions in our daily routines, influencing how we perceive time management and punctuality.
And if you really want to talk about an indispensable companion in our daily routine, you might have one in your pocket, the mobile phone.

records.transcript: Today we are discussing the concept of dark stores. That is, retail centers that resemble warehouses and are usually located near city centers. Unlike traditional storefronts, they are not designed for walk in customers, but function as fulfillment hubs optimized for rapid online delivery. The rise of dark stores has been fueled by the growing demand for online shopping, especially in urban areas where space is limited and rent is high. The main appeal of dark stores lies in their efficiency. By eliminating the traditional storefront, businesses can reduce overhead costs and pass savings on to consumers through lower prices. Their proximity to dense urban areas also allows for faster delivery times, meeting the expectations of customers who value speed and convenience. For instance, a company might deliver groceries in under an hour, giving it a major competitive advantage over traditional supermarkets. However, dark stores are not without drawbacks. Their expansion can contribute to the decline of traditional retail spaces, creating economic challenges for local businesses. Employment is another concern. While these centers generate jobs in logistics and delivery, they may reduce the number of customer facing roles available in physical stores. Looking ahead, many experts predict that dark stores will continue to reshape the retail landscape. Some may adopt advanced automation, further reducing the need for human labor and potentially redefining the shopping experience itself. As with other technological shifts, the key challenge will be balancing efficiency with the broader social and economic implications of these changes.

今天我们来讨论“暗店”的概念。
也就是说，它们是类似于仓库的零售中心，通常位于市中心附近。
与传统店面不同，它们不是为上门顾客设计的，而是作为优化了快速在线配送的履约中心运作。

通过取消传统店面，企业可以降低运营成本，并通过更低的价格将节省下来的钱惠及消费者。

例如，一家公司可以在一小时内配送杂货，这使其比传统超市具有主要的竞争优势。
然而，暗店并非没有缺点。
它们的扩张可能导致传统零售空间的衰落，给当地企业带来经济挑战。

展望未来，许多专家预测暗店将继续重塑零售格局。
一些暗店可能会采用先进自动化，进一步减少对人力的需求，并可能重新定义购物体验本身。
与其他技术变革一样，主要挑战将是平衡效率与这些变革更广泛的社会和经济影响。

records.transcript: Back in the mid 1800s, scientists dredging the ocean floor stumbled on previously unknown life forms: brittle stars, sea cucumbers, even deep sea corals, creatures living in pitch darkness, near freezing water, and under crushing pressure. That discovery flipped the old belief that such conditions couldn't support life. But what do these organisms eat? Near the ocean surface, food chains begin with phytoplankton, tiny plants that use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide into energy. These phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed fish, and these in turn feed larger predators. But in the deep ocean, sunlight doesn't reach, so phytoplankton cannot grow there. Instead, many deep sea organisms depend on something called marine snow. It is a constant shower of organic matter: dead plankton, bits of decaying creatures, and animal waste products, all sinking from above. But marine snow does more than feed deep sea life. It carries carbon from surface waters down to the deep sea floor, where some of it can stay locked away for centuries, even millennia. This process helps regulate Earth's climate by pulling carbon from surface waters, and so out of the atmosphere, which interacts with the surface waters. As you probably know, carbon in the atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide gas, has a warming effect on Earth's climate, and the extra carbon released from human activities has caused dangerous global warming. How much carbon does marine snow remove? Roughly 10 billion tons annually, about the same as all human cars.
records.translation:
回到19世纪中期，科学家们在疏浚海底时，偶然发现了以前未知的生命形式：海蛇尾、海参，甚至深海珊瑚，这些生物生活在漆黑、接近冰点的水和巨大的压力之下。
这一发现颠覆了此前认为这种条件无法支持生命的旧观念。
但是这些生物吃什么呢？
在海洋表面附近，食物链始于浮游植物，这些微小的植物利用阳光将二氧化碳转化为能量。
这些浮游植物喂养浮游动物，浮游动物喂养鱼类，而鱼类又喂养更大的捕食者。
但在深海，阳光无法到达，因此浮游植物无法在那里生长。
相反，许多深海生物依赖于一种叫做“海洋雪”的东西。
它是有机物质的持续“降雪”：死亡的浮游生物、腐烂生物的碎片和动物排泄物，都从上方沉降下来。
但海洋雪不仅仅为深海生物提供食物。
它将碳从表层水域带到深海海底，其中一部分碳可以被封存数百年，甚至数千年。
这个过程通过将碳从表层水域，从而从与表层水域相互作用的大气中抽取出来，帮助调节地球的气候。
正如你可能知道的，大气中的碳，以二氧化碳气体的形式存在，对地球气候有增温效应，而人类活动释放的额外碳已导致危险的全球变暖。
海洋雪能去除多少碳？
每年大约100亿吨，与所有人类汽车的排放量大致相同。

transcriptSentences.text: Back in the mid 1800s, scientists dredging the ocean floor stumbled on previously unknown life forms: brittle stars, sea cucumbers, even deep sea corals, creatures living in pitch darkness, near freezing water, and under crushing pressure.
That discovery flipped the old belief that such conditions couldn't support life.
But what do these organisms eat?
Near the ocean surface, food chains begin with phytoplankton, tiny plants that use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide into energy.
These phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed fish, and these in turn feed larger predators.
But in the deep ocean, sunlight doesn't reach, so phytoplankton cannot grow there.
Instead, many deep sea organisms depend on something called marine snow.
It is a constant shower of organic matter: dead plankton, bits of decaying creatures, and animal waste products, all sinking from above.
But marine snow does more than feed deep sea life.
It carries carbon from surface waters down to the deep sea floor, where some of it can stay locked away for centuries, even millennia.
This process helps regulate Earth's climate by pulling carbon from surface waters, and so out of the atmosphere, which interacts with the surface waters.

As you probably know, carbon in the atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide gas, has a warming effect on Earth's climate, and the extra carbon released from human activities has caused dangerous global warming.
How much carbon does marine snow remove?
Roughly 10 billion tons annually, about the same as all human cars.

records.transcript: The Galapagos Islands, a popular tourist attraction located approximately 1,000 kilometers off mainland Ecuador, have long been home to many interesting species of animals, including giant tortoises. Historically, these reptiles could be found on many different Galapagos Islands, but in some of these locations, they've gone extinct, due in part to human activities. To deal with this situation, conservationists employed a strategy called animal translocation to move tortoises from one island to another. So, why did conservationists do this? The main reason was to promote ecosystem recovery on affected islands. One place tortoises went extinct was on Santa Fe Island. When these reptiles died out, the island was without its main ecosystem engineer. This affected the island in many ways, including causing plant diversity to decline. To help the ecosystem recover, conservationists have released more than 400 tortoises from Espanola Island onto Santa Fe Island. This was done to help restore natural processes like seed dispersal and vegetation control. The goal is to reach about 4,000 individuals to match historical densities. And there are signs that this project is having success. For example, a type of cactus that many animals on the island rely on for food has shown improved reproduction and growth since the tortoises returned. This is no doubt because tortoises eat this cactus's fruit and spread seeds in their nutrient rich droppings. This finding is encouraging, but we can't declare the project a victory yet. More time needs to pass before conservationists can deem it a success.

records.transcript: There are many different factors that influence human behavior. One is related to social influence, or the idea that our behavior can be shaped by group pressure. To test this idea, a psychologist named Solomon Asch conducted a famous study in the 1950s which has become hugely influential in the field. In his experiment, Asch invited American university students to take part in a simple visual judgment task. Each participant was placed in a group of seven to nine people, all but one of whom were working with the researcher. The group members were shown a standard line on one card and three comparison lines on another card. One comparison line matched the standard, while the other two were clearly different lengths. Basically, the correct choice was totally obvious. Each person announced aloud which line matched the standard, and those who were in on the study deliberately gave the wrong answer first. The real participant answered last. Across 12 trials, seventy five percent of participants conformed with the incorrect answers that people in the group had given before them at least once. So they chose the line that was clearly wrong. This indicates the strong influence of group pressure. This study was replicated in 1980, roughly 30 years after Asch conducted his experiment. The subjects in this experiment were British university students. Interestingly, conformity was much lower with these participants. This suggests that conformity may be influenced by culture and the country people grow up in.
records.translation:
影响人类行为的因素有很多。
其中之一与社会影响有关，或者说，我们的行为可以由群体压力塑造。

在他的实验中，阿施邀请美国大学生参加一个简单的视觉判断任务。
每个参与者被分到一个由七到九人组成的小组，其中除了一个外，其他人都在与研究人员合作。
小组成员看到一张卡片上有一条标准线，另一张卡片上有三条比较线。
其中一条比较线与标准线匹配，而另外两条则明显长度不同。
基本上，正确的选择是完全明显的。
每个人都大声宣布哪条线与标准线匹配，而那些参与研究的人故意先给出错误的答案。
真正的参与者最后回答。
在12次试验中，75%的参与者至少有一次顺从了小组中其他人给出的错误答案。
所以他们选择了明显错误的线条。
这表明了群体压力的强大影响。
这项研究在1980年被复制，大约在阿施进行实验30年后。
这项实验的受试者是英国大学生。
有趣的是，这些参与者的从众性要低得多。
这表明从众行为可能受到文化和人们成长国家的双重影响。

transcriptSentences.text: There are many different factors that influence human behavior.
One is related to social influence, or the idea that our behavior can be shaped by group pressure.
To test this idea, a psychologist named Solomon Asch conducted a famous study in the 1950s which has become hugely influential in the field.
In his experiment, Asch invited American university students to take part in a simple visual judgment task.
Each participant was placed in a group of seven to nine people, all but one of whom were working with the researcher.
The group members were shown a standard line on one card and three comparison lines on another card.
One comparison line matched the standard, while the other two were clearly different lengths.
Basically, the correct choice was totally obvious.
Each person announced aloud which line matched the standard, and those who were in on the study deliberately gave the wrong answer first.
The real participant answered last.

records.transcript: Imagine you're a painter. Now, would your passion for painting be driven purely by internal motivation? In other words, would you paint just for the joy of it? What if you were being paid for your paintings? Intuitively, we might assume that an external reward or financial incentive would amplify your motivation. But that's not the case. Paradoxically, the opposite often occurs: a phenomenon known in psychology as the overjustification effect. Intrinsic motivation decreases when external incentives come into play. Consider an experiment from the 1970s. Children who naturally gravitated toward drawing with markers were observed. Some children were promised rewards for their drawings. Then, during free time, the group that expected rewards spent significantly less time drawing compared to other kids, suggesting that extrinsic rewards can lower an individual's interest. The underlying mechanism here is a perceived shift in autonomy. So take an activity that's initially pursued just for the fun of it. Introduce an external reward, and individuals feel their actions are no longer self driven but driven by the reward itself. The activity feels more like an obligation than a passion. And you can imagine implications across various fields, education and business, where encouraging intrinsic motivation is crucial. Students or employees who are rewarded for activities they already enjoy could lose their natural enthusiasm over time. Understanding the overjustification effect can help us when we're creating settings intended to nurture, not suppress, intrinsic motivation.

records.transcript: I'm sure you are familiar with ostriches, the large flightless birds of Africa, and you've heard of Australian emus. There are several species of large flightless birds on different continents. They're all from the same group, called paleognaths, and are genetically related, meaning they're descendants of the same ancestral species that evolved over time into the present day species. But how did they end up on different continents? One theory was rooted in Earth's geohistory. You see, until 175 million years ago, Earth's continents were all together as one giant supercontinent. Later, they slowly drifted apart. So maybe the paleognaths' flightless ancestral species lived on that supercontinent, and the descendants evolved into separate species after it split into today's land masses. However, recent genetic research found that the ancestral paleognath hadn't appeared until many millions of years after the supercontinent had already broken apart. There goes that idea. So how did the birds end up this way? Well, in 2025, researchers studied the fossilized breastbone of an ancient paleognath called Lithornis, which could be the ancestor of today's paleognaths. From its shape, they determined that Lithornis could fly great distances. It must have established populations in Africa, Australia, and elsewhere. Initially, Lithornis used flight to escape predatory dinosaurs, but after the dinosaurs went extinct, it no longer needed to waste its energy flying. It could use its specialized beak to find food on the ground. Over time, on each different land mass, its descendant species lost the ability to fly.

在不同大陆上都有几种大型不会飞的鸟类。
它们都来自同一个群体，被称为古颚鸟类，并且在基因上是相关的，这意味着它们是同一个祖先物种的后代，随着时间演变成了今天的物种。
