records.transcript: During the Roman Empire, soldiers had a lot of, uh, weapons and armor, and they needed a place to store them. Their arms and armor. Soldiers used boxes called armariums to store this gear. Armariums were big, portable wooden storage boxes. Later, people, including civilians, kept using armariums in their homes, but to store items like clothing, books, or other valuables. In France in the 16th century, wealthy people had them and called them armoires. Armoire is a term we still use today for a large, standalone piece of wooden furniture for storing things. Around the same time, some homes in England started to have what they called closets. But these closets were more like, uh, small studies where people could store things, or also just read or be alone. Someone might play their guitar in one to relax. So both the armoire and the English closet, they were kind of precursors to the modern closet. If we fast forward to the mid 1800s, in the early United States, we're starting to see closets that are built directly into homes as part of the floor plan. The big benefit of these was that they were less pricey than armoires. Way cheaper. People had less clothing then than they do today, and they'd usually use a small chest to store clothes, or hang them on a peg or hook. Coat hangers weren't invented until the late 1800s. But still, closets in the home were handy places to store other belongings.

records.transcript: When I was growing up, Pluto was known as the ninth planet in our solar system. Alas, Pluto was demoted to dwarf planet status in 2006, and not only because it's so small, maybe half the width of the United States. It's mainly because in 2006, it was decided that planets had to meet three criteria. They had to orbit the Sun and be round in shape. Check and check. But they also had to be the main object in their orbit. Which, well, Pluto is in the Kuiper Belt. The Kuiper Belt contains many other bodies that orbit the Sun, so Pluto lost its planet status as a result. Many scientists dismissed Pluto as just a ball of ice anyway. However, about ten years later, the New Horizons spacecraft sent back new images and data showing that Pluto is far more complex than previously thought. We're talking volcanoes and dunes. I mean, get this: Pluto has a deep basin with three types of ice, and New Horizons' images suggest there's convection in the basin of ice. With convection, warmer ice rises to the surface, then cools and sinks at the edge of the basin. So the surface is continuously rejuvenating, renewing itself. Moreover, under the basin of ice there may be something astonishing: a saltwater ocean. Life could exist there. records.transcript: Ever wonder why some rewards motivate better than others when you’re trying to change behavior? Most people think of rewards as tangible things: money, candy, gift cards. These are what psychologists call extrinsic rewards because they come from an external source. But in the 1960s, psychologist David Premack had a different idea. Instead of giving people tangible things, why not use activities people already enjoy? This became Premack’s principle. Here are the basics. You can use something someone already likes to do, or a high probability behavior to motivate an activity they avoid or a low probability behavior. Here’s an example. If a child loves playing outside but hates cleaning their room, you make outdoor play the reward for cleaning. First clean, then play. It’s simple but powerful. Premack believed this strategy works better than candy or money, because it motivates by tapping into what psychologists call intrinsic rewards, things that feel good because we genuinely enjoy them. Tangible rewards often lose their appeal, but favorite activities stay motivating. By linking something less appealing to something naturally fun, you create a lasting incentive that feels personal and meaningful. Think about it. If you’re trying to get yourself to the gym more often, you might promise yourself extra time on a hobby you love after your workout. You’re not bribing yourself with something artificial or external. You’re connecting the new habit to something that already matters to you. That’s why Premack’s principle is still relevant today, and not just for parents and teachers.

records.transcript: Back in 1938, a chemist named Roy Plunkett was working to create a new refrigerant, a new cooling substance. Plunkett was looking for an industrial refrigerant to replace the ones that existed at the time, which were toxic and flammable. Some, for example, could cause fatal poisoning if leaked. He was working with a gas called tetrafluoroethylene, or TFE, a highly flammable refrigerant. Plunkett stored TFE gas in cylinders, but one day he noticed that a cylinder of TFE no longer had gas in it. What was there? Well, powder, a solid. The TFE gas had solidified into this new powdery substance, polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. What made PTFE remarkable was its almost unprecedented stability, its resistance to heat, chemicals, and friction. It didn’t react with other substances, making it ideal for industrial applications like parts used in the aerospace industry, also medical devices and electronics. Eventually, PTFE began to be used in consumer products. Ever heard of Teflon, the nonstick coating on frying pans? That was PTFE and it was used in homes around the world for many years. These days you may be more likely to use stainless steel or cast iron cookware due to concerns with PTFE. Nevertheless, this is a classic example of serendipity in science. Plunkett wasn’t trying to invent a non stick surface. He stumbled upon it. This kind of discovery isn’t rare. Scientists discovered X rays, penicillin and many other scientific and medical innovations while trying to do something else.

例如，有些制冷剂一旦泄漏可能导致致命中毒。

嗯，是粉末，一种固体。

records.transcript: You’ve probably used many remote controls for things like televisions, smart devices, and other electronics. My wife uses one to open the gate to her parking lot at work. Now, remote controls for TV’s have been around since the 1950s. Wired remote controls had been used before then, back to around 1870, mostly for unpiloted, uh, military vehicles. Later, the inventor Nikola Tesla developed a wireless remote control for military vehicles in 1898. As for TV remotes, the first really popular one was developed in 1950. It was called the Lazy Bones and was pretty expensive. Unfortunately, the Lazy Bones was connected to the TV by a long wire, which of course was annoying and a trip hazard. It’s kind of hard to imagine this was more practical for most people than just getting up and turning the dial on the television yourself. A few years later, in 1955, a wireless remote was introduced, the Flash Matic. To use the Flash Matic, you’d point it at one of the corners of your TV screen. This would shine a light beam at the chosen corner. Now, each corner had its own purpose: channel up or down, power, or mute. Each corner had a photoelectric cell to convert the light beam into an electrical signal to do what you want. Trouble was, the photoelectric cells responded to other light sources too, like from a light bulb or even sunlight. Imagine turning on a light bulb and your TV suddenly turns on too.

records.transcript: David Hockney, one of Britain’s most celebrated painters, is renowned for his use of bold color and constant experimentation. In the 1960s, he gained fame with large acrylic paintings of California swimming pools, works like A Bigger Splash, which captured light, leisure, and everyday moments from modern life with striking clarity. Throughout his career, Hockney embraced innovation, always exploring how technology could expand his artistic vision. Decades later, in 2009, that curiosity led him to digital art. He began on a mobile phone, drawn at first to its portability and ease of use. Digital painting offered freedoms unimaginable with oil paints or even acrylic paints: no drying time, no storage issues and infinite color choices at the tap of his fingers. Hockney used these features to create vibrant landscapes and intimate still lifes, often sharing them instantly with friends, a spontaneity that echoed his lifelong interest in technology’s role in art. Working on a small screen shaped his style, simplified forms, luminous colors and a fluid process that felt like a dialogue with light and time. Eventually, he moved to a tablet where a larger screen allowed broader gestures, richer details and more complex compositions. These works retained his fascination with the theme of daily life, but now they also reflected the freedoms of the digital medium: bolder colors, more clarity and freshness. Hockney’s digital paintings remind us that while tools evolve, art’s essence remains, seeing the world always in a new light.
records.translation:
大卫·霍克尼，英国最著名的画家之一，以其大胆的色彩运用和不断的实验而闻名。
20世纪60年代，他以加州游泳池的大幅丙烯画作而闻名，如《更大的水花》等作品，以惊人的清晰度捕捉了现代生活中的光线、闲暇和日常瞬间。
霍克尼在他的整个职业生涯中都拥抱创新，不断探索技术如何拓展他的艺术视野。
几十年后，在2009年，这种好奇心将他引向了数字艺术。
他最初从手机开始创作，起初是被其便携性和易用性所吸引。
数字绘画提供了油画甚至丙烯画都无法想象的自由：无需干燥时间，没有存储问题，只需轻触指尖即可获得无限的色彩选择。
霍克尼利用这些特点创作了充满活力的风景画和亲密的静物画，并经常立即与朋友分享，这种自发性呼应了他对技术在艺术中作用的毕生兴趣。
在小屏幕上创作塑造了他的风格：简化的形式、明亮的色彩和一种流畅的过程，感觉就像与光线和时间的对话。
最终，他转向了平板电脑，更大的屏幕允许更宽广的笔触、更丰富的细节和更复杂的构图。
这些作品保留了他对日常生活主题的迷恋，但现在它们也反映了数字媒介的自由：更大胆的色彩、更高的清晰度和新鲜感。
霍克尼的数字绘画提醒我们，尽管工具不断发展，艺术的本质依然存在，它总是以新的视角看待世界。

records.transcript: Today I want to talk about an animal whose building skills have fascinated scientists and architects alike: termites. Now, when most people hear the word termite, they think of an insect that damages wooden houses. But some termite species, especially those in dry regions of Africa and Australia, construct enormous mounds that are astonishingly sophisticated. These mounds are not just piles of soil. They are carefully organized structures with tunnels, chambers, and ventilation shafts. What is most impressive is that the insects build them without any central plan or leader. Each termite responds to local cues, such as temperature, humidity, and chemical signals left by other termites. The result is a structure that can help maintain a stable internal environment even when outdoor temperatures change dramatically. Inside many termite mounds, the colony must keep conditions suitable for the termites themselves and, in some species, for fungus that the termites cultivate as food. The mound helps regulate temperature and air flow. Warm air rises through central channels and exits near the top, while cooler air is drawn in through lower openings. In addition, the thick outer walls absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. This means that the interior can remain relatively steady, even when the outside environment becomes very hot during the day and cool at night. Of course, these structures face challenges. Heavy rains can damage the walls, and strong winds can wear away the mound's surface. Termites constantly repair and modify their mounds in response to changing conditions. In fact, the mound is not a finished building in the way a human house is. It is more like a living system that is continually adjusted by thousands or even millions of insects. Architects have paid attention to termite mounds because they suggest ways to design human buildings that use less energy. If a building can be cooled partly through natural air circulation instead of relying entirely on air conditioning, it can save a great deal of energy. So termites remind us that complex design does not always require a single designer. Sometimes simple responses by many individuals can produce a remarkably effective structure.
records.translation:
今天我想谈论一种动物，它们的建筑技能让科学家和建筑师都为之着迷：白蚁。
现在，当大多数人听到“白蚁”这个词时，他们会想到一种会破坏木制房屋的昆虫。
但是有些白蚁种类，尤其是非洲和澳大利亚干旱地区的白蚁，会建造出令人惊叹的、极其复杂的巨大蚁丘。
这些蚁丘不仅仅是泥土堆。
它们是精心组织的结构，包含隧道、巢室和通风井。
最令人印象深刻的是，这些昆虫在没有任何中央计划或领导者的情况下建造了它们。
每只白蚁都会对局部线索做出反应，例如温度、湿度以及其他白蚁留下的化学信号。
结果是，即使外部温度剧烈变化，这种结构也能帮助维持稳定的内部环境。
在许多白蚁丘内部，蚁群必须保持适合白蚁自身以及（在某些物种中）适合白蚁作为食物培养的真菌的条件。
蚁丘有助于调节温度和气流。
暖空气通过中央通道上升并从顶部附近排出，而冷空气则通过下部开口吸入。
此外，厚厚的外壁白天吸收热量，夜间缓慢释放。
这意味着即使外部环境白天非常热、夜间很冷，内部也能保持相对稳定。
当然，这些结构也面临挑战。
大雨会损坏墙壁，强风会磨损蚁丘表面。
白蚁会根据不断变化的条件持续修复和改造它们的蚁丘。
事实上，蚁丘不像人类的房屋那样是已完工的建筑。
它更像一个由成千上万甚至数百万昆虫不断调整的生命系统。
建筑师们一直关注白蚁丘，因为它们为设计能耗更低的人类建筑提供了思路。
如果建筑物可以通过自然空气循环部分冷却，而不是完全依赖空调，它就能节省大量能源。
所以白蚁提醒我们，复杂的设计不总是需要一个单独的设计师。
有时，许多个体的简单反应就能产生极其有效的结构。

transcriptSentences.text: Today I want to talk about an animal whose building skills have fascinated scientists and architects alike: termites.
Now, when most people hear the word termite, they think of an insect that damages wooden houses.
But some termite species, especially those in dry regions of Africa and Australia, construct enormous mounds that are astonishingly sophisticated.
These mounds are not just piles of soil.
They are carefully organized structures with tunnels, chambers, and ventilation shafts.
What is most impressive is that the insects build them without any central plan or leader.
Each termite responds to local cues, such as temperature, humidity, and chemical signals left by other termites.
The result is a structure that can help maintain a stable internal environment even when outdoor temperatures change dramatically.
Inside many termite mounds, the colony must keep conditions suitable for the termites themselves and, in some species, for fungus that the termites cultivate as food.
The mound helps regulate temperature and air flow.
Warm air rises through central channels and exits near the top, while cooler air is drawn in through lower openings.
In addition, the thick outer walls absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night.
This means that the interior can remain relatively steady, even when the outside environment becomes very hot during the day and cool at night.
Of course, these structures face challenges.
Heavy rains can damage the walls, and strong winds can wear away the mound's surface.
Termites constantly repair and modify their mounds in response to changing conditions.
In fact, the mound is not a finished building in the way a human house is.
It is more like a living system that is continually adjusted by thousands or even millions of insects.
Architects have paid attention to termite mounds because they suggest ways to design human buildings that use less energy.
If a building can be cooled partly through natural air circulation instead of relying entirely on air conditioning, it can save a great deal of energy.
So termites remind us that complex design does not always require a single designer.
Sometimes simple responses by many individuals can produce a remarkably effective structure.

records.transcript: Today we're going to look at the history of blue pigment and why the color blue has held such a special place in art. This may seem surprising, since blue is everywhere in nature: the sky, the ocean, distant mountains. But for much of human history, a stable and brilliant blue pigment was actually difficult to obtain. Because it was rare and expensive, blue often became associated with wealth, importance, and spiritual value. One of the most famous sources of blue pigment was lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone mined mainly in what is now Afghanistan. To make the pigment known as ultramarine, artists or specialists had to grind the stone and separate the blue mineral from impurities. The process was labor intensive, and the material traveled long distances before reaching European workshops. So ultramarine could cost more than gold. During the Renaissance, patrons sometimes specified in contracts exactly how much ultramarine an artist was required to use, especially in paintings of the Virgin Mary. The blue cloak in such paintings was not just a color choice; it signaled devotion, prestige, and the patron's willingness to pay for the finest materials. But the use of blue changed over time. As new pigments became available, especially synthetic blues, artists no longer had to reserve blue for the most sacred or wealthy subjects. Prussian blue, discovered in the early eighteenth century, was cheaper and easier to produce. Later, other synthetic blues expanded the palette even further. This changed both artistic practice and public access to blue. Blue could appear more freely in landscapes, decorative objects, printed materials, and eventually everyday products. Even so, some artists and collectors continued to prefer lapis lazuli. Why? Partly because of its extraordinary depth and slight variation in tone. Synthetic pigments could be consistent and practical, but lapis had a history and a visual richness that some people felt could not be fully replaced. So the story of blue pigment is not simply a story of technology replacing older materials. It is also about symbolism, economics, and the emotional value people attach to a color.
records.translation:
今天我们将探讨蓝色颜料的历史，以及为什么蓝色在艺术中占据如此特殊的地位。
这可能令人惊讶，因为蓝色在大自然中随处可见：天空、海洋、远山。
但在人类历史的大部分时间里，稳定而鲜艳的蓝色颜料实际上很难获得。
因为它稀有而昂贵，蓝色常常与财富、重要性和精神价值联系在一起。
最著名的蓝色颜料来源之一是青金石，一种主要在今天的阿富汗开采的深蓝色石头。
为了制造被称为群青的颜料，艺术家或专家必须研磨石头，并将蓝色矿物质与杂质分离。
这个过程是劳动密集型的，而且这种材料在运到欧洲作坊之前要经过长途跋涉。
所以群青的成本可能比黄金还高。
在文艺复兴时期，资助人有时会在合同中明确规定艺术家需要使用多少群青，尤其是在绘制圣母玛利亚的画作中。
此类画作中的蓝色斗篷不仅仅是一种颜色选择；它象征着虔诚、声望和资助人愿意为最好的材料买单的意愿。
但蓝色的使用随着时间而改变。
随着新颜料的出现，尤其是合成蓝色颜料，艺术家不再需要将蓝色保留给最神圣或最富有的主题。
普鲁士蓝，在18世纪早期被发现，更便宜也更容易生产。
后来，其他合成蓝色颜料进一步拓宽了调色板。
这改变了艺术实践和公众对蓝色的使用。
蓝色可以更自由地出现在风景画、装饰品、印刷材料，并最终出现在日常产品中。
即便如此，一些艺术家和收藏家仍然喜欢青金石。
为什么？
部分原因在于其非凡的深度和细微的色调变化。
合成颜料可以保持一致和实用，但青金石拥有历史和视觉上的丰富性，有些人觉得这些是无法完全取代的。
因此，蓝色颜料的故事不仅仅是技术取代旧材料的故事。
它也关乎象征意义、经济学以及人们赋予一种颜色的情感价值。

records.transcript: Today we'll examine how the Industrial Revolution reshaped European cities. Before industrialization, many European cities still had features that dated back to the medieval period: narrow streets, defensive walls, and neighborhoods organized around markets, churches, or craft workshops. But industrialization changed both the economy and the physical layout of cities. Factories needed workers, access to transportation, and space for machinery. As a result, populations grew rapidly, and cities expanded beyond their older boundaries. One of the most visible changes was the removal of city walls. Originally, walls had been built for defense, but by the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries they often limited expansion and interfered with transportation. Industrial cities needed rail lines, wider roads, canals, and later streetcar routes. Old walls were frequently demolished so that goods and workers could move more efficiently. The land where walls had stood was sometimes converted into boulevards, parks, or new commercial districts. Industrial workplaces also changed the daily experience of urban life. In earlier craft production, work often took place in small workshops or even in the home. With industrialization, large numbers of workers traveled to factories according to a more rigid schedule. This contributed to the separation of residential, industrial, and commercial areas. Working class housing often developed near factories because workers needed to live close to their jobs, but these neighborhoods could be crowded and polluted. Smoke from factories, waste from production, and poor sanitation created serious public health problems. The street layout of industrial cities changed too. Wider streets and more regular grids were introduced in some places to improve traffic flow and allow carts, carriages, and later public transit to move more easily. These changes had consequences beyond transportation. They encouraged the growth of commercial centers and made it easier for city governments to provide services such as lighting, sewers, and police patrols. So when we study industrial cities, we are not just studying factories. We are studying how economic change altered space, movement, health, and daily life.
records.translation:
今天我们将探讨工业革命是如何重塑欧洲城市的。
在工业化之前，许多欧洲城市仍然保留着可以追溯到中世纪的特征：狭窄的街道、防御城墙，以及围绕市场、教堂或手工作坊组织的社区。
但是工业化改变了经济和城市的物理布局。
工厂需要工人、便利的交通以及放置机器的空间。
结果，人口迅速增长，城市扩展到了旧有的边界之外。
最显著的变化之一是拆除城墙。
最初，城墙是为防御而建的，但到了18世纪和19世纪，它们经常限制城市的扩张并妨碍交通。
工业城市需要铁路线、更宽的道路、运河，以及后来的有轨电车路线。
旧城墙经常被拆除，以便货物和工人能够更高效地移动。
城墙曾经矗立的土地有时被改造成林荫大道、公园或新的商业区。
工业工作场所也改变了城市生活的日常体验。
在早期的手工生产中，工作通常在小作坊甚至家里进行。
随着工业化，大量工人按照更严格的时间表前往工厂上班。
这促成了住宅区、工业区和商业区的分离。
工人阶级的住房通常在工厂附近发展，因为工人需要住得离工作地点近，但这些社区可能很拥挤且污染严重。
工厂的烟雾、生产废料和恶劣的卫生条件造成了严重的公共卫生问题。
工业城市的街道布局也发生了变化。
一些地方引入了更宽的街道和更规则的网格布局，以改善交通流量，并使手推车、马车以及后来的公共交通工具能够更顺畅地移动。
这些变化的影响超出了交通领域。
它们鼓励了商业中心的增长，并使市政府更容易提供照明、下水道和警察巡逻等服务。
因此，当我们研究工业城市时，我们不仅仅是在研究工厂。
我们是在研究经济变革如何改变了空间、交通、健康和日常生活。

transcriptSentences.text: Today we'll examine how the Industrial Revolution reshaped European cities.

Before industrialization, many European cities still had features that dated back to the medieval period: narrow streets, defensive walls, and neighborhoods organized around markets, churches, or craft workshops.
But industrialization changed both the economy and the physical layout of cities.
Factories needed workers, access to transportation, and space for machinery.
As a result, populations grew rapidly, and cities expanded beyond their older boundaries.
One of the most visible changes was the removal of city walls.
Originally, walls had been built for defense, but by the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries they often limited expansion and interfered with transportation.
Industrial cities needed rail lines, wider roads, canals, and later streetcar routes.
Old walls were frequently demolished so that goods and workers could move more efficiently.
The land where walls had stood was sometimes converted into boulevards, parks, or new commercial districts.
Industrial workplaces also changed the daily experience of urban life.
In earlier craft production, work often took place in small workshops or even in the home.
With industrialization, large numbers of workers traveled to factories according to a more rigid schedule.
This contributed to the separation of residential, industrial, and commercial areas.
Working class housing often developed near factories because workers needed to live close to their jobs, but these neighborhoods could be crowded and polluted.
Smoke from factories, waste from production, and poor sanitation created serious public health problems.
The street layout of industrial cities changed too.
Wider streets and more regular grids were introduced in some places to improve traffic flow and allow carts, carriages, and later public transit to move more easily.
These changes had consequences beyond transportation.
They encouraged the growth of commercial centers and made it easier for city governments to provide services such as lighting, sewers, and police patrols.
So when we study industrial cities, we are not just studying factories.
We are studying how economic change altered space, movement, health, and daily life.

Today, we're going to focus on people who combine that entrepreneurial spirit with social impact. I'm talking about social entrepreneurs. These are individuals who seek to solve societal problems through innovative and sustainable business solutions. Unlike traditional entrepreneurs, their primary goal is not simply to make money. They also strive to stimulate positive changes in society. Now, one of the key features of social entrepreneurship is a focus on addressing gaps in the market that affect underserved communities. This can include anything from providing affordable healthcare and education to developing environmentally friendly technologies. Social entrepreneurs often work in sectors where social needs are most pressing. For example, many social enterprises aim to tackle issues related to poverty, health, and the environment. They do so by leveraging business strategies to create scalable and sustainable solutions to these problems. As you can imagine, social entrepreneurship can be quite challenging. After all, balancing profitability with social goals can be complex and demanding. Also, measuring the social impact of an initiative is not an easy undertaking. Just what should be measured? Worst of all, these ventures often require significant resources and support to get off the ground. Despite these obstacles, the potential benefits of social entrepreneurship are immense. It can lead to innovative solutions that traditional businesses might overlook and foster a more inclusive and equitable society.

records.transcript: Humans have been expressing themselves through art for thousands of years. Consider ancient cave paintings that have been discovered throughout the world, some of them more than 40,000 years old. Caves in Sulawesi, Indonesia, that include figurative art, are an example of this. Some forms of art, though, have much more recent origins. Take, for example, decalcomania, a really cool art technique that originated in the 18th century. So what is decalcomania? At its core, it's a simple process. You begin by spreading paint onto a surface like a sheet of paper. Then you press another surface, let's say canvas, onto the paper. So you press the two surfaces together. At this point, you pull them apart while the paint is still wet. The resulting image is often rich with organic, abstract patterns. Decalcomania was first used to decorate pottery in the 18th century, but it really took off in the 20th century, especially with the surrealist movement. Artists like Max Ernst loved this technique, because it helped them tap into the subconscious and explore the unexpected. Ernst was enchanted by the process that allowed him to create shapes that the artist could not fully control. What's especially intriguing about decalcomania is the balance it strikes between control and chaos. Sure, the artist chooses the colors and the materials, but once the process is complete, the final result is mostly up to chance.

印度尼西亚苏拉威西岛的洞穴中包含具象艺术，就是一个例子。
然而，有些艺术形式的起源要晚得多。
例如，拓印画，一种非常酷的艺术技巧，起源于18世纪。
那么，什么是拓印画呢？
从本质上讲，这是一个简单的过程。
你首先将颜料涂抹到像纸张这样的表面上。
然后你将另一个表面，比如说画布，压到纸上。
所以你把两个表面压在一起。
这时，趁颜料还湿的时候，你将它们分开。
由此产生的图像通常充满了有机、抽象的图案。
拓印画最初在18世纪用于装饰陶器，但在20世纪真正流行起来，尤其是在超现实主义运动中。
马克斯·恩斯特等艺术家热爱这种技巧，因为它帮助他们深入潜意识，探索意想不到的事物。

当然，艺术家选择颜色和材料，但一旦过程完成，最终结果大多取决于偶然性。

records.transcript: Kinship refers to the relationships formed through blood ties, marriage, or adoption. When you think about siblings or parent and child, you're thinking about consanguineal relationships, those based on shared blood. In contrast, relationships formed through marriage, such as the bond between spouses or between a person and their in laws, are known as affinal relationships. Both types of relationships play important roles. Kinship systems vary widely across cultures. Some societies practice patrilineal descent, where lineage and inheritance are traced through the father's side of the family. Others follow matrilineal descent, where these aspects are traced through the mother's side. How do anthropologists study kinship? They often live within a community for extended periods to conduct interviews, attend family events, and make observations. An anthropologist studying a matrilineal society might observe the role of maternal uncles, who may play key roles in child rearing. Anthropologists map out relationships in kinship charts to visualize how people are related and to identify patterns in descent, marriage, and inheritance. Do kinship charts sound like family trees to you? Well, they both illustrate relationships among people. Family trees are commonly used in genealogy to trace biological ancestry and family history, while kinship charts highlight cultural categories of kin as well as biological ties. For example, in some cultures, a mother's sister may be treated as a second mother, and this relationship would be represented accordingly in a kinship chart.

records.transcript: Imagine taking a regular piano and transforming its sound by inserting everyday objects like screws, bolts, and rubber erasers between the strings. This is what's known as a prepared piano. It was developed by the avant garde composer John Cage in 1940. Cage was working at a university in Seattle, and he needed to write music with percussion to accompany dancers. But the performance space's stage wasn't big enough for percussion instruments like drums. So he made the sounds with just the piano by placing objects between the strings. Now, Cage spent time searching for items that made the kind of sounds he was looking for. It had a feel of improvisation. Cage himself said that looking for items was kind of like walking on the beach and looking for shiny or beautiful seashells that you liked. That is, he didn't know ahead of time what items he wanted to use. He just kept looking around and seeing what suited his needs. Cage ended up composing a collection of music for prepared piano in the mid 1940s. He included specific instructions for how to prepare the piano. For this collection, Cage was inspired by ancient Hindu theory and about eight essential emotions. He wanted his listeners to sense eight essential emotions from Hindu philosophy. The result is a blending of sounds that would be familiar to a Western audience, plus sounds reminiscent of Indonesian gamelan. Gamelan is traditional Indonesian percussion music. This prepared piano music really raised John Cage's profile in the music world.

这就是所谓的预置钢琴。
它是由前卫作曲家约翰·凯奇于1940年发明的。
凯奇当时在西雅图的一所大学工作，他需要创作带有打击乐的音乐来为舞者伴奏。

也就是说，他事先并不知道自己想用什么物品。
他只是不断地四处寻找，看看什么适合他的需求。

records.transcript: Have you ever stared at a blank page, trying to come up with an idea of what to write about, waiting for inspiration? Storytelling dice are a simple way to break through that creative block. Yes, I'm talking about dice similar to ones you roll in some common board games to generate random numbers. But instead of numbers, each die is covered with pictorial symbols, like a tree, a key, or a lightning bolt. A typical set could have nine six sided dice. The magic lies in their unpredictability. You might roll a dragon, a locked door, and a storm. Suddenly, you're weaving a tale of, say, hidden realms and daring escapes. Storytelling dice are not just for writers. They can also serve as icebreakers at social gatherings. Imagine this: The party feels a little stiff, so you pull out the dice and say: Everyone, roll three. Someone gets a dragon, a ladder, and a smiley face. Another rolls a spaceship, shoes, and a storm cloud. Soon, people are laughing as they connect these random images into a wild story. The dragon was stuck on a ladder during a thunderstorm. And then a spaceship landed to rescue it. It's silly, spontaneous, and gets everyone talking. But now, let's get back to creative writing and talk about a short story that a previous student of mine wrote last semester. While reading the story, try to guess what three images she rolled on her dice that inspired her to write it.

records.transcript: Today I'd like to talk about the color blue in art. Now, we might take blue for granted, but for centuries it was one of the most elusive and expensive pigments an artist could use. In ancient Egypt, artisans crafted blue from lapis lazuli, a brilliant stone mined in what is now Afghanistan. This mineral was so rare and so valuable that it was literally worth its weight in gold. Because of its scarcity, blue was reserved for the most honored subjects in art. In medieval European paintings, important holy figures were often cloaked in deep blue robes. This wasn't just symbolic, it was also a financial statement. During the Renaissance, oil paints made it easier to mix and layer colors, including lapis lazuli powder with oil. Still, blue remained costly due to its natural sources. Then came a turning point in the 18th century: synthetic dyes. Prussian blue, which was originally created in Germany quite by accident, was affordable, vibrant, and widely accessible. Suddenly, artists from all walks of life could use blue freely. The democratization of color transformed artistic expression and opened doors for artistic movements like impressionism, where blue was used freely to evoke mood, atmosphere, and emotion. Even today, blue carries echoes of its luxurious past. It's often linked to ideas of calm, depth, and aspiration. Yet some traditionalists still argue that no synthetic pigment can match the richness and depth of lapis lazuli. The story of blue continues to reflect the evolving relationship between art, innovation, and culture.
records.translation:
今天我想谈谈艺术中的蓝色。
现在，我们可能认为蓝色是理所当然的，但几个世纪以来，它一直是艺术家所能使用的最难以捉摸和昂贵的颜料之一。
在古埃及，工匠们用青金石制作蓝色，这是一种在今天的阿富汗开采的闪亮石头。
这种矿物如此稀有和珍贵，以至于它的价值真的相当于其重量的黄金。
由于其稀缺性，蓝色被保留用于艺术中最受尊敬的主题。
在中世纪欧洲的绘画中，重要的神圣人物常常身披深蓝色长袍。
这不仅仅是象征性的，也是一种财富的体现。
文艺复兴时期，油画使得混合和分层颜色变得更容易，包括将青金石粉末与油混合。
尽管如此，由于其天然来源，蓝色仍然昂贵。
然后在18世纪迎来了转折点：合成染料。
普鲁士蓝，最初在德国纯属偶然被创造出来，价格实惠、色彩鲜艳且易于获取。
突然之间，各行各业的艺术家都可以自由使用蓝色了。
色彩的民主化改变了艺术表现形式，为印象派等艺术运动打开了大门，在印象派中，蓝色被自由地用于唤起情绪、氛围和情感。
即使在今天，蓝色仍然承载着其奢华过去的余韵。
它常与平静、深度和抱负的理念联系在一起。
然而，一些传统主义者仍然认为，没有任何合成颜料能够与青金石的丰富性和深度相媲美。
蓝色的故事继续反映着艺术、创新和文化之间不断演变的关系。

transcriptSentences.text: Today I'd like to talk about the color blue in art.
Now, we might take blue for granted, but for centuries it was one of the most elusive and expensive pigments an artist could use.
In ancient Egypt, artisans crafted blue from lapis lazuli, a brilliant stone mined in what is now Afghanistan.
This mineral was so rare and so valuable that it was literally worth its weight in gold.
Because of its scarcity, blue was reserved for the most honored subjects in art.
In medieval European paintings, important holy figures were often cloaked in deep blue robes.
This wasn't just symbolic, it was also a financial statement.
During the Renaissance, oil paints made it easier to mix and layer colors, including lapis lazuli powder with oil.
Still, blue remained costly due to its natural sources.
Then came a turning point in the 18th century: synthetic dyes.
Prussian blue, which was originally created in Germany quite by accident, was affordable, vibrant, and widely accessible.
Suddenly, artists from all walks of life could use blue freely.
The democratization of color transformed artistic expression and opened doors for artistic movements like impressionism, where blue was used freely to evoke mood, atmosphere, and emotion.
Even today, blue carries echoes of its luxurious past.
It's often linked to ideas of calm, depth, and aspiration.
Yet some traditionalists still argue that no synthetic pigment can match the richness and depth of lapis lazuli.
The story of blue continues to reflect the evolving relationship between art, innovation, and culture.

records.transcript: Previously, we discussed the significance of pottery to ancient cultures, including pottery as an art form and pottery's crucial role in trade. Today, we'll focus on the development of pottery over time. One breakthrough was the invention of the potter's wheel, around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia. Before this, pottery was shaped mostly by hand, which was slow and produced less uniform results. The potter's wheel allowed artisans to spin and shape the clay more quickly and evenly, making it possible to create symmetrical vessels with greater precision and speed. Firing technology also advanced. Early pots were fired in open pits, which limited temperature control, resulting in uneven or fragile pots. So kilns were developed, enclosed ovens that could reach higher and more consistent temperatures. These allowed for stronger, more durable pottery. Another advance was the updraft kiln, which directed heat upward through the chamber. By adjusting the airflow, potters could control how much oxygen reached the fire. This helped them produce pottery with specific colors like red or black, depending on how the clay reacted to the firing atmosphere. Then, in ancient China, potters developed kilns that could reach very high temperatures. This allowed them to create stoneware and eventually porcelain. Porcelain is made from a special mix of fine clay and minerals, and must be fired at temperatures above 1,200 degrees Celsius. The result is a smooth, white ceramic that is strong, lightweight, and slightly translucent. Porcelain was a major breakthrough because it was more durable and versatile than earlier pottery.

records.transcript: For decades, archaeologists believed that complex societies and the monumental architecture, the large buildings, signifying them, only emerged after agriculture. And that farming was essential for societal development. After all, before agriculture developed, people tended not to settle in a single place, but moved from place to place in search of food. We call such people nomadic hunter gatherers. They were continuously on the move to hunt and collect food. And for people who aren't settled, it was more practical to live in small mobile groups rather than in complex societies. Or so it was believed. But the excavation of the ancient site of Göbekli Tepe threw a wrench in this whole story. Göbekli Tepe, dating back about 11,000 years, consists of multiple massive pillars arranged in circles and is considered the world's oldest known temple. Remarkably, it predates the earliest evidence of agriculture in the area by several thousand years. This suggests spiritual practices, not agriculture, may have caused early communities to form. Many scholars interpret the site as a ceremonial center, a periodic gathering place for nomadic hunter gatherers. More recently, archaeologists there did find traces of things like food processing areas, stone tools for grinding grains, as well as actual plant residues. Yet these residues come from local wild grains, not domesticated crops. And the structures may not indicate year round habitation. So while Göbekli Tepe might have hosted temporary gatherings, the evidence still supports the idea that spiritual practices played a central role in early societal development.
records.translation:
几十年来，考古学家一直认为，复杂的社会以及象征它们的宏伟建筑（大型建筑）只有在农业出现之后才出现。
而且农业对社会发展至关重要。
毕竟，在农业发展之前，人们往往不安定居在一个地方，而是四处迁徙寻找食物。
我们称这些人是游牧的狩猎采集者。
他们不断地迁徙以狩猎和采集食物。
对于不安定居的人来说，生活在小型流动群体中比生活在复杂社会中更实际。
至少之前是这样认为的。
但是格贝克利石阵古遗址的挖掘却给这个故事带来了意想不到的转折。
格贝克利石阵可追溯到大约11,000年前，由多个圆形排列的巨大石柱组成，被认为是世界上已知最古老的寺庙。
值得注意的是，它比该地区最早的农业证据早了几千年。
这表明是精神实践而非农业，可能导致了早期社区的形成。
许多学者将该遗址解释为一个仪式中心，一个游牧狩猎采集者定期聚集的场所。
最近，那里的考古学家确实发现了食物加工区、研磨谷物的石器以及实际植物残骸的痕迹。
然而，这些残骸来自当地的野生谷物，而非驯化作物。
而且这些结构可能并不表明是全年居住地。
因此，尽管格贝克利石阵可能举办过临时集会，但证据仍然支持精神实践在早期社会发展中扮演核心角色的观点。

transcriptSentences.text: For decades, archaeologists believed that complex societies and the monumental architecture, the large buildings, signifying them, only emerged after agriculture.
And that farming was essential for societal development.
After all, before agriculture developed, people tended not to settle in a single place, but moved from place to place in search of food.

They were continuously on the move to hunt and collect food.

records.transcript: Today, let's talk about the effects of the Industrial Revolution on urban life in Europe. Last week, we talked about how between the 16th and the 19th centuries, industrial capitalism utterly changed the European economy. As manufacturing became the most profitable activity, cities naturally grew larger and took on a new character. By 1850, the physical layout of an industrial city was completely different from that of its predecessors. How do we picture a medieval city? It's surrounded by walls to protect it from invasion from the neighboring city. The emergence of nation states did away with this need for protection from invasion, at least on the city scale. And so, over the centuries, the walls were removed and city boundaries pushed out dramatically. Industrial workplaces had been small craft shops, but now they were huge factories located in large factory districts, with separate housing for workers constructed nearby. Medieval street layouts that had developed haphazardly were built over, replaced by a gridiron street pattern. Each lot was uniform and predictable, which made it easier to buy and sell property. Many cities kept their central marketplaces, but commercial structures became more and more common. Commerce became more prominent in city centers, often more so than cathedrals. Manchester, England, is a good example of this. It grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution, and commercial buildings dominated the city center. Its layout reflected the new priorities of industrial capitalism.

records.transcript: Imagine you’re a painter. Now, would your passion for painting be driven purely by internal motivation? In other words, would you paint just for the joy of it? What if you’re being paid for your paintings? Intuitively, we might assume that an external reward or financial incentive would amplify your motivation, but that’s not the case. Paradoxically, the opposite often occurs, a phenomenon known in psychology as the overjustification effect. Intrinsic motivation decreases when external incentives come into play. Let me describe an experiment from the 1970s. Children who naturally gravitated toward drawing with markers were observed. Some children were promised rewards for their drawings. Then, during free time, the group that expected rewards spent significantly less time drawing compared to other kids, suggesting that extrinsic rewards can lower an individual’s interest. The underlying mechanism here is a perceived shift in autonomy. So, take an activity that’s initially pursued just for the fun of it, introduce an external reward and individuals feel their actions are no longer self driven, but driven by the reward itself. The activity feels more like an obligation than a passion. And you can imagine implications across various fields, education, business, where encouraging intrinsic motivation is crucial. Students or employees who are rewarded for activities they already enjoy could lose their enthusiasm over time. Understanding the overjustification effect can help us when we’re creating settings intended to nurture, not suppress, intrinsic motivation.

records.transcript: Welcome to Science in Motion, the show where we explore the hidden physics behind everyday experiences. Today, we're investigating why ice skating feels so smooth and fluid. The answer lies in a fascinating physical phenomenon that's happening right beneath your feet. When a skate blade moves across the ice, it's not just slicing through a frozen surface; it's actually causing a tiny bit of it to melt. The pressure from the blade creates a thin layer of water between the skate and the ice. This slippery film is what allows skaters to move so gracefully. It's called the pressure melting point, and it means that ice can melt at temperatures below freezing simply because of the force being applied. As the skater moves, the blade keeps applying pressure, maintaining this delicate balance between solid and liquid. However, friction between the blade and the ice can also generate heat. Too much heat, and the ice melts more than it should, slowing skaters down or even causing them to lose control. That's why elite skaters develop techniques to minimize friction. In addition, researchers are studying these dynamics to design skate blades that reduce friction and boost performance. But the story doesn't end at the rink. Similar principles are at play in nature, specifically in glaciers. Pressure and melting help these massive ice sheets move across landscapes. As scientists dig deeper into how these mechanisms work, they're learning how glaciers might respond to climate change, offering clues about our planet's future.

records.transcript: Earlier in class, we talked about the Dutch tulip craze of the early 1600s, a time when tulip bulbs became luxury symbols, prices soared, and fortunes vanished almost overnight. It was one of history's first economic bubbles, fueled by speculation and status. America had its own version in the early 19th century when the country was swept up in the mulberry craze. The idea sounded simple. Plant mulberry trees, raise the silkworms that eat their leaves, collect the silk from the worm's cocoons, and rake in the profits. Silk was a prized luxury import and producing it locally promised enormous wealth. Farmers and investors rushed to buy mulberry saplings. Prices for the young trees soared from pennies to several dollars. Classic bubble behavior. And the speculation wasn't all about money. Silk itself, the idea of silk, carried powerful symbolism: refinement, status, and aspiration. For a brief moment, middle class Americans imagined silk dresses as attainable, blurring old class distinctions. But reality intervened. records.transcript: Desertification is the process by which fertile land transforms into desert, typically as a result of drought, deforestation, or unsustainable agricultural practices. One significant driver of desertification is the overexploitation of land for intensive agriculture. This can exhaust soil nutrients, diminish vegetation cover, and accelerate erosion. Without root systems to anchor the soil, wind and water strip away topsoil, leaving behind barren land. In some cases, monoculture farming and excessive irrigation also contribute by disrupting natural soil chemistry. Deforestation further intensifies desertification. When forests are cleared for timber or agricultural expansion, the absence of trees reduces the land's capacity to retain moisture. This loss of canopy cover not only dries out the soil, but also disrupts local rainfall patterns, compounding the desert spread. Climate change is another accelerating force. Rising global temperatures and shifting precipitation cycles lead to prolonged droughts and extreme weather events, placing additional stress on soil and vegetation. Once fertile regions are becoming increasingly arid and agriculturally unviable. Desertification can trigger food and water insecurity, and species adapted to specific soil and moisture conditions may struggle to survive. Mitigation efforts include sustainable land management, reforestation, and soil restoration initiatives. Projects like the Great Green Wall in Africa aim to reverse degradation by planting trees and creating green jobs. Addressing desertification is essential not only for environmental health, but also for the stability and resilience of human communities worldwide.
records.translation:
荒漠化是指肥沃土地变为沙漠的过程，通常是由于干旱、森林砍伐或不可持续的农业实践造成的。
荒漠化的一个重要驱动因素是为集约农业对土地的过度开发。
这会耗尽土壤养分，减少植被覆盖，加速侵蚀。
没有根系固定土壤，风和水会冲刷掉表层土壤，留下贫瘠的土地。
在某些情况下，单一作物种植和过度灌溉也通过破坏自然土壤化学成分而起到推波助澜的作用。
森林砍伐进一步加剧了荒漠化。
当森林被砍伐用于木材或农业扩张时，树木的缺失会降低土地保持水分的能力。
这种树冠覆盖的丧失不仅使土壤干燥，还会扰乱当地的降雨模式，加剧沙漠的蔓延。
气候变化是另一个加速因素。
全球气温上升和降水周期变化导致长期干旱和极端天气事件，给土壤和植被带来了额外压力。
曾经肥沃的地区正变得越来越干旱，不适合农业生产。
荒漠化可能引发粮食和水资源不安全，适应特定土壤和水分条件的物种可能难以生存。
缓解措施包括可持续土地管理、重新造林和土壤恢复倡议。
非洲的“绿色长城”等项目旨在通过植树造林和创造绿色就业来扭转土地退化。
应对荒漠化不仅对环境健康至关重要，也对全球人类社区的稳定性和韧性至关重要。

records.transcript: Have you ever wondered how music influences our eating habits? Well, it turns out the kind of music playing in the background when we dine can significantly shape our culinary experience. Recent research has demonstrated that fast music, music with a rapid tempo, can make us eat more quickly, while slower tunes encourage us to savor our meals. And, you know, my doctor's been telling me eating slowly is good for digestion and health. It's important to chew the food well. Anyway, music isn't just about speed. It's about taste perception as well. For instance, a study found that high pitched music can enhance the sweetness of a dish, while a lower pitch might accentuate its bitterness. Restaurants have started to take note of these findings and are curating playlists to improve their patrons' dining experiences. This auditory seasoning, as some call it, is becoming an essential part of the ambiance. Now, some argue that this manipulation can detract from the authenticity of the food experience. It can make diners more susceptible to overeating or misjudging the quality of their meal. This isn't just theory. Take the example of a high end restaurant that experimented with soundscapes. By playing ocean sounds, they found that diners rated seafood dishes more favorably, feeling as if they were right by the sea. While this kind of thing might revolutionize dining, some diners may prefer a more genuine taste experience, free from any auditory influence.

records.transcript: During the early 20th century, technology was advancing rapidly, and music was no exception. Today, we're talking about electrophones, the predecessors of today's synthesizers. These early electronic instruments challenged musical conventions by creating sound not through vibrating strings or air columns, but through electronic means. One of the earliest and most famous electrophones is the theremin, which creates melodies through the manipulation of electromagnetic fields. The musician doesn't even touch the instrument. Instead, hand movements near two metal antennas control pitch and volume. Its eerie tones soon became associated with experimental compositions. Another important instrument was the Ondes Martenot, developed in France. It gave composers a wider expressive range and could be played by gliding a ring along a wire, kind of like moving a bow across violin strings. Together, the theremin and the Ondes Martenot set the stage for later synthesizers, which now dominate everything from pop to film scores. So while early electrophones may seem unusual today, they were crucial in making new musical ideas possible. They left a lasting mark on how people think about creating sound.
records.translation:
在20世纪早期，科技发展迅速，音乐也不例外。
今天，我们来谈谈电声乐器（electrophones），它们是现代合成器的前身。
这些早期的电子乐器挑战了音乐传统，它们不通过振动的琴弦或空气柱来发声，而是通过电子手段。
最早也是最著名的电声乐器之一是特雷门琴，它通过操纵电磁场来创造旋律。
音乐家甚至都不需要触碰这种乐器。
相反，在两根金属天线附近的手部动作控制着音高和音量。
它那空灵怪异的音色很快就与实验性作曲联系在了一起。
另一种重要的乐器是在法国发明的马特诺琴。
它为作曲家提供了更广阔的表现空间，可以通过沿着一根金属线滑动一个圆环来演奏，有点像用琴弓在小提琴琴弦上拉动。
特雷门琴和马特诺琴一起为后来的合成器奠定了基础，而现在的合成器主导着从流行音乐到电影配乐的各个领域。
因此，尽管早期的电声乐器在今天看来可能有些不同寻常，但它们在使新的音乐理念成为可能方面发挥了至关重要的作用。
它们在人们如何看待声音创作方面留下了持久的印记。

transcriptSentences.text: During the early 20th century, technology was advancing rapidly, and music was no exception.
Today, we're talking about electrophones, the predecessors of today's synthesizers.
These early electronic instruments challenged musical conventions by creating sound not through vibrating strings or air columns, but through electronic means.
One of the earliest and most famous electrophones is the theremin, which creates melodies through the manipulation of electromagnetic fields.
The musician doesn't even touch the instrument.
Instead, hand movements near two metal antennas control pitch and volume.
Its eerie tones soon became associated with experimental compositions.
Another important instrument was the Ondes Martenot, developed in France.
It gave composers a wider expressive range and could be played by gliding a ring along a wire, kind of like moving a bow across violin strings.
Together, the theremin and the Ondes Martenot set the stage for later synthesizers, which now dominate everything from pop to film scores.
So while early electrophones may seem unusual today, they were crucial in making new musical ideas possible.
They left a lasting mark on how people think about creating sound.

records.transcript: Researchers are studying how sensory experiences can affect human behavior, like the use of ambient scent. Ambient scent is the strategic use of a certain fragrance, smell, in a space to set a specific mood, for example, or to cause people to associate a scent with a particular brand. Like a hotel chain, and each hotel's lobby smells like, say, pine trees. Customers experience that ambient scent every time they enter one of these hotels, and it can increase their loyalty to that hotel chain. One experiment involved participants in a room that smelled like freshly baked cookies, while others were in a scentless environment. Those who had the pleasant aroma around them were significantly more likely to volunteer for a charitable cause later. It's as if the warm and inviting scent triggered a sense of goodwill and community feeling in these participants. Why does this happen? Well, scents stimulate our limbic system. The limbic system is the part of the brain that's responsible for emotions and memory. So, fragrances can really make our brains connect with our emotional state and access our memories. When we encounter a comforting smell, like fresh bread, it might remind us of home or childhood, nudging us toward kindness and cooperation. The implications of this are intriguing, especially in marketing or organizational behavior. Imagine using lavender, which has a calming effect, in a high pressure work environment. Something as simple as smell can have a profound effect on actions and decisions.
records.translation:
研究人员正在研究感官体验如何影响人类行为，例如环境气味的使用。
环境气味是指在某个空间中策略性地使用某种香气或气味，例如，营造特定的氛围，或者让人们将某种气味与某个特定品牌联系起来。
就像一个连锁酒店，每家酒店的大堂都闻起来像松树。
顾客每次进入这些酒店时都会体验到这种环境气味，这可以增加他们对该酒店连锁的忠诚度。
一个实验让参与者在一个闻起来像新鲜出炉的饼干的房间里，而另一些人则在一个无气味的环境中。
那些周围有宜人香气的人后来更乐意为一个慈善事业做志愿者。
就好像温暖宜人的气味触发了这些参与者的善意和社区归属感。
为什么会发生这种情况呢？
嗯，气味会刺激我们的边缘系统。
边缘系统是大脑中负责情感和记忆的部分。

records.transcript: One growing concern in marine biology is ocean acidification. This refers to the decrease in the pH of Earth's oceans, mainly due to the absorption of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, which lowers the pH and alters the ocean's chemical balance. This change has serious consequences for marine organisms, especially those that use calcium carbonate to build shells and skeletons, such as staghorn corals, Pacific oysters, and certain types of plankton. As acidity increases, these organisms struggle to maintain their structures, resulting in weaker shells and unhealthy corals. Coral reefs, such as the Great Barrier Reef in the Coral Sea, are particularly vulnerable. Their decline can lead to reduced biodiversity and disrupted ecosystems. Ocean acidification also affects fish. A 2023 study conducted by marine biologists at James Cook University found that clown fish exposed to lower pH levels in reef environments had difficulty detecting the sounds of predators and navigating their surroundings. This sensory impairment may also interfere with reproduction, threatening population stability. To address this issue, efforts focus on reducing carbon dioxide emissions. This includes shifting to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and adopting sustainable practices. Additionally, protecting ecosystems like seagrass beds and mangroves can help absorb carbon dioxide and buffer acidification. Mangroves, in particular, can store up to ten times more carbon per hectare than terrestrial forests. Understanding and mitigating ocean acidification is essential for preserving marine biodiversity and maintaining healthy oceans. It requires global cooperation and long term commitment.
records.translation:
海洋生物学中一个日益受到关注的问题是海洋酸化。
这指的是地球海洋pH值的下降，主要是由于吸收了大气中的二氧化碳。
当二氧化碳溶解在海水中时，会形成碳酸，从而降低pH值并改变海洋的化学平衡。
这种变化对海洋生物有严重的后果，特别是那些利用碳酸钙构建壳和骨骼的生物，如鹿角珊瑚、太平洋牡蛎和某些类型的浮游生物。
随着酸度增加，这些生物难以维持其结构，导致外壳变弱和珊瑚不健康。
珊瑚礁，如珊瑚海的大堡礁，尤其脆弱。
它们的衰退会导致生物多样性减少和生态系统遭到破坏。
海洋酸化也影响鱼类。
詹姆斯库克大学的海洋生物学家在2023年进行的一项研究发现，暴露在礁石环境中较低pH值的海葵鱼难以探测到捕食者的声音并导航周围环境。
这种感官障碍也可能干扰繁殖，威胁种群稳定。
为了解决这个问题，努力的重点是减少二氧化碳排放。
这包括转向可再生能源、提高能源效率和采用可持续做法。
此外，保护海草床和红树林等生态系统有助于吸收二氧化碳并缓冲酸化。
特别是红树林，每公顷储存的碳量是陆地森林的十倍。
了解和缓解海洋酸化对于保护海洋生物多样性和维持健康的海洋至关重要。
这需要全球合作和长期承诺。

records.transcript: Today, let's talk about the ancient Maya civilization and explore a fascinating revelation about its decline. A vast civilization with impressive cities and flourishing culture that suddenly crumbled into history. For years, scholars have debated what might have happened, and now recent research has brought stalagmites into the spotlight. Stalagmites, those formations rising up from the floor of a cave, are more than just geological wonders. They serve as climate records, capturing changes in precipitation over thousands of years. In 2025, scientists analyzed stalagmites from caves near the former Maya heartlands. The data revealed a series of prolonged droughts that coincided with periods of decline for the Maya society. Now, Maya were heavily dependent on agriculture, with water being a critical resource for their survival. When these droughts occurred, the scarcity of water likely put immense pressure on their food production and societal structures. Imagine cities struggling without enough water for crops, leading to food shortages and social unrest. It's important to note, though, that while these climate changes were significant, they weren't the sole cause. Other factors, like warfare and politics, played a role, too. Yet the revelation from these stalagmites provides a clearer picture of how environmental changes can trigger societal shifts. This discovery not only sheds light on the past, but also serves as a reminder of our vulnerability to climate change today.

records.transcript: By the year 600 CE, writers would make pens out of feathers, which they dipped in ink. Interestingly, the technology didn't change a whole lot over a thousand years. Then, in the 1930s, a Hungarian newspaper editor named László Bíró was getting frustrated. He had to do a lot of handwriting for his job, but the pens he wrote with would leave smudges. The ink would splatter. Yuck! He also noted how his newspapers were printed. Newsprint ink didn't smudge, but it dried right away. Now, László Bíró was lucky enough to have a brother who had studied chemistry. They worked together to come up with a ballpoint pen design that could use ink, like what was used on newsprint. Eventually, they came up with a pen that housed a little steel ball in a socket and a small ink barrel that could hold ink paste. It might sound simple, but there was a lot of work involved in figuring out the right size and shape for the components, the composition of the ink, et cetera. Later, Bíró tweaked the pen design not to rely on gravity, so you could hold the pen at different angles and it'd still work. Unfortunately, this was expensive. It wasn't until the 1950s that a French entrepreneur, uh, he improved the design of the ballpoint pen and made it super cheap to make. This is the kind of pen still sold today and which you have most likely seen and used.
records.translation:
到公元600年，作家们会用羽毛制作蘸墨水用的笔。
有趣的是，这项技术在一千多年里都没有发生太大变化。
然后，在20世纪30年代，一位名叫拉斯洛·比罗的匈牙利报纸编辑感到很沮丧。
他的工作需要大量手写，但他用的笔会留下污迹。
墨水会飞溅。
真糟糕！
他还注意到报纸是如何印刷的。
报纸油墨不会弄脏，而且会立刻变干。
现在，拉斯洛·比罗很幸运，他有一个学习化学的兄弟。
他们一起设计出了一种圆珠笔，可以使用报纸上用的那种墨水。
最终，他们发明了一种笔，笔内有一个小钢珠，嵌在一个插座里，还有一个可以装墨水膏的小墨水管。
这听起来可能很简单，但在确定部件的正确尺寸和形状、墨水的成分等方面，需要做大量的工作。
后来，比罗改进了笔的设计，使其不依赖重力，这样你就可以以不同的角度握笔，它仍然能工作。
不幸的是，这很昂贵。
直到20世纪50年代，一位法国企业家才改进了圆珠笔的设计，使其制造成本变得非常低廉。
这种笔至今仍在销售，你很可能见过并使用过。

transcriptSentences.text: By the year 600 CE, writers would make pens out of feathers, which they dipped in ink.
Interestingly, the technology didn't change a whole lot over a thousand years.
Then, in the 1930s, a Hungarian newspaper editor named László Bíró was getting frustrated.

Yuck!

Now, László Bíró was lucky enough to have a brother who had studied chemistry.

Eventually, they came up with a pen that housed a little steel ball in a socket and a small ink barrel that could hold ink paste.
It might sound simple, but there was a lot of work involved in figuring out the right size and shape for the components, the composition of the ink, et cetera.
Later, Bíró tweaked the pen design not to rely on gravity, so you could hold the pen at different angles and it'd still work.
Unfortunately, this was expensive.
It wasn't until the 1950s that a French entrepreneur, uh, he improved the design of the ballpoint pen and made it super cheap to make.

records.transcript: Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available. Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and converts it to electricity or heat. The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them. The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero harmful pollutants. Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels. But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Another advantage, and one we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas, far from the grid. So what are the disadvantages? Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which of course reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels. That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non sunny periods. Panel lifespan is quite good at 25 to 30 years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that, so waste is increasing faster than expected. This is a problem because recycling them is expensive, and most panels end up in landfills.
records.translation:
接下来，在我们的可再生能源系列中，我们将讨论太阳能，这可以说是最丰富的可用资源。
太阳能从太阳光线中获取能量，并将其转化为电能或热能。
其主要技术是由光伏电池组成的太阳能电池板，当阳光照射到电池板上时，会产生电流。
太阳能的优点众所周知，其中最重要的一点可能是它不会产生任何有害污染物。
任何工业活动都会以这样或那样的方式产生二氧化碳，制造太阳能电池板本身就需要消耗化石燃料产生的能量。
但总的来说，这个行业的碳足迹远低于煤炭或天然气，这使得它成为减少温室气体排放的关键。
另一个优点，也是我们谈论不够多的一个，是太阳能可以在偏远和服务不足的地区提供能源，远离电网。
那么缺点是什么呢？
太阳能电池板的效率受到云层覆盖和其他天气的影响，这当然会减少到达电池板的阳光量。
尽管如此，电池储能系统的创新确实允许储存太阳能，以便在非晴朗时期使用。
电池板的寿命相当好，有25到30年，但效率的提高却矛盾地导致电池板比预期更早地被更换，因此废物增加的速度超过了预期。
这是一个问题，因为回收它们成本高昂，而且大多数电池板最终都会进入垃圾填埋场。

transcriptSentences.text: Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available.
Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and converts it to electricity or heat.
The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them.
The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero harmful pollutants.
Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels.
But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Another advantage, and one we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas, far from the grid.
So what are the disadvantages?
Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which of course reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels.
That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non sunny periods.
Panel lifespan is quite good at 25 to 30 years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that, so waste is increasing faster than expected.
This is a problem because recycling them is expensive, and most panels end up in landfills.

records.transcript: Last week, we talked about realism, in which artists aimed to depict the world as it really exists. Today, we'll explore surrealism. Starting in France in the 1920s, surrealist artists focused on inner realities, concepts such as fantasy and the nature of dreams. Their works reflected a combination of these inner realities as well as outer realities, that is, things we physically experience. Their paintings often depicted a familiar scene, but in a dreamlike manner. Spaniard Joan Miro was especially adept at surrealism. Interestingly, though, Miro never wanted to be associated with any artistic movement, and he never called himself a surrealist. But his contemporaries did, and we can see why they did when we look at Miro's work. Miro typically painted in two stages. The latter stage was carefully calculated. It was meticulous and precise. Miro knew exactly what he was doing in this stage. But in the initial stage, Miro didn't plan what he was going to paint. He just started painting. The form, whatever it was, a bird, a building, whatever appeared on the canvas, the form suggested itself under his brush. That's how Miro described it. This method of creating art without conscious control is called automatism. Automatism is quite noticeable in a work of Miro's that is titled, simply, Painting. Even Miro couldn't fully explain the meaning of this work. Miro's painting was a form of self reflection. Presumably, the images that appeared came from things deep inside him. Things he may not have even known were there.
records.translation:
上周我们讨论了现实主义，其中艺术家旨在描绘世界真实存在的样子。
今天，我们将探索超现实主义。
超现实主义艺术家从20世纪20年代的法国开始，专注于内在现实，例如幻想和梦的本质等概念。
他们的作品反映了这些内在现实以及外在现实的结合，即我们身体上体验到的事物。
他们的画作经常描绘熟悉的场景，但以一种梦幻般的方式。
西班牙人胡安·米罗尤其擅长超现实主义。
然而有趣的是，米罗从不想与任何艺术运动联系在一起，他也从未称自己为超现实主义者。
但他的同时代人却这样做了，当我们看到米罗的作品时，我们就能明白他们为什么这样做。
米罗通常分两个阶段作画。
后一个阶段是精心计算的。
它一丝不苟，精确无误。
米罗在这个阶段确切地知道自己在做什么。
但在最初阶段，米罗并没有计划他要画什么。
他只是开始画画。
形状，无论是什么，一只鸟，一栋建筑，无论出现在画布上什么，形状都在他的画笔下自行显现。
米罗就是这样描述它的。
这种在没有意识控制下创作艺术的方法被称为自动主义。
自动主义在米罗的一幅名为《绘画》的作品中非常明显。
即使是米罗也无法完全解释这幅作品的含义。
米罗的绘画是一种自我反思的形式。
据推测，出现的图像来自他内心深处的东西。
他可能甚至不知道它们在那里。

transcriptSentences.text: Last week, we talked about realism, in which artists aimed to depict the world as it really exists.
Today, we'll explore surrealism.
Starting in France in the 1920s, surrealist artists focused on inner realities, concepts such as fantasy and the nature of dreams.
Their works reflected a combination of these inner realities as well as outer realities, that is, things we physically experience.

Spaniard Joan Miro was especially adept at surrealism.

records.transcript: Social networks are not just digital online platforms. They're fundamental to understanding how people connect and interact. One powerful tool for analyzing these networks is the sociogram. A sociogram is a visual map that charts relationships within a group. It looks a little like a spider's web. Sociograms illustrate who interacts with whom, how frequently and in what patterns, and by making invisible social structures visible, they reveal dynamics such as influence, isolation, and centrality. Rather than focusing on individual behavior as traditional studies would, sociograms emphasize the web of connections that shape group outcomes. In classrooms, they can identify students who are socially isolated or those who act as bridges between different social groups. In workplaces, sociograms help uncover informal hierarchies and where communication breaks down. In public health, they're used to trace contact patterns and predict how diseases might spread from person to person. Sociograms are valuable in marketing as well, where understanding who influences purchasing decisions can guide advertising strategy. However, sociograms do have limitations. By reducing relationships to lines in a web of interactions, they may overlook the subtleties of human interactions, such as trust, conflict, or emotional intensity that aren't easily captured in a diagram. Understanding these qualitative aspects often requires complementary methods like interviews or observation to fully appreciate. Still, when used thoughtfully and alongside other tools, sociograms remain a vital resource for visualizing and analyzing social networks. Their strength lies in turning abstract social dynamics into concrete, interpretable visuals, making them indispensable across disciplines.

社交网络不仅仅是数字化的在线平台。
它们对于理解人们如何连接和互动至关重要。
分析这些网络的一个强大工具是社会关系图（sociogram）。
社会关系图是一种视觉地图，它描绘了一个群体内的关系。
它看起来有点像蜘蛛网。
社会关系图描绘了谁与谁互动，互动的频率和模式，通过使无形的社会结构变得可见，它们揭示了诸如影响力、孤立和中心性等动态。
社会关系图并非像传统研究那样关注个体行为，而是强调塑造群体结果的连接网络。
在课堂上，它们可以识别出那些社会孤立的学生，或者那些在不同社交群体之间充当桥梁的学生。
在工作场所，社会关系图有助于揭示非正式的等级制度以及沟通中断的地方。
在公共卫生领域，它们被用来追踪接触模式，并预测疾病如何在人与人之间传播。
社会关系图在市场营销中也很有价值，了解谁影响购买决策可以指导广告策略。
然而，社会关系图确实有局限性。
通过将关系简化为互动网络中的线条，它们可能会忽视人类互动的微妙之处，例如信任、冲突或情感强度，这些都无法轻易地在图表中捕捉到。
理解这些定性方面往往需要访谈或观察等补充方法才能充分理解。
尽管如此，当深思熟虑地使用并与其他工具结合时，社会关系图仍然是可视化和分析社交网络的重要资源。
它们的优势在于将抽象的社会动态转化为具体、可解释的视觉图像，使其在各个学科中都不可或缺。

records.transcript: Today I've got a topic that might just electrify your imagination. Lightning in the atmosphere of Venus. You might wonder why we should care about lightning on another planet. Well, understanding lightning on Venus could give us clues about the planet's dynamic weather systems. Okay, so the Soviet Venera space missions set out to explore Venus, one of Earth's closest neighbors. What these missions found was surprising. Evidence of lightning in Venus's thick, sulfuric, acid laden clouds. So picture this. The sky is perpetually cloaked in clouds. Lightning flickers through the gloom. It's practically the setting for a science fiction movie. But this isn't fiction. It's real science. And here's where it gets interesting. The presence of lightning suggests that the atmosphere of Venus is more dynamic than we once assumed. Why does this matter? Lightning can play a crucial role in atmospheric chemistry, affecting the formation of molecules and influencing weather patterns. On Earth, lightning is known to create compounds like nitrogen oxides, which are essential for plant life. While Venus doesn't have plant life, understanding its atmospheric processes helps scientists build models that can be applied to other planets, including our own. Moreover, studying Venusian lightning can help us predict future changes in its atmosphere. If lightning is as prevalent as the Venera mission suggests, it could mean that Venus is more geologically active than previously assumed. This suggests new ideas for research. Could other planets with similar conditions harbor surprising phenomena? Or even forms of life?

records.transcript: One tool that's useful in many fields is a Geographical Information System, or GIS. GIS is a computer system that can collect and, uh, store lots of data about specific locations. GIS software can also analyze and display data. You're probably familiar with GPS, which also uses location data. GPS is used for navigation and positioning, and it relies on hardware like satellite, right? Our phones use it. We use GPS on our phones to get directions to places. On the other hand, GIS is software based and is used for making decisions. Picture a trucking company delivering furniture. They'd use GPS to track where trucks are and where they're headed. The company might use GIS, though, to analyze the amount of fuel that trucks use on particular routes. They'd analyze traffic patterns, elevation changes, things like that, to make decisions about shipping routes. Geographers can use GIS to study the interactions between humans and the environment. Say some farms start using a new fertilizer. GIS can analyze the location of those farms, including nearby streams. GIS can then analyze rainfall patterns in those locations. By combining and analyzing all these data, GIS helps researchers predict where the fertilizer is likely to wind up polluting a stream. Quite useful. GIS software can also create maps of important buildings and sites in historic districts of cities, then assess for things like how development nearby would impact the historic district. This aids with conservation and managing these important locations.

records.transcript: Can food plus waste products trigger algal blooms? Algal blooms are rapid increases in algae, tiny aquatic plants that can cloud the water. When those algal blooms die off, they decompose and deplete oxygen from the water, which can suffocate fish and other aquatic life. Of course, the main cause of algal blooms is chemical fertilizers in agricultural runoff, like when water from rain or irrigation flows over fields and carries the fertilizers to rivers and coastal waters. But fish farming causes algal blooms too. An intriguing alternative is or was the coastal fish ponds of ancient Hawaii called Lokoiya. People in Hawaii are reviving them today. These ponds, built along the shore using mainly lava, captured nutrient rich runoff from nearby fields, naturally fertilizing the ponds. This was before the days of concentrated artificial fertilizers. Instead of causing algal blooms, the nutrients supported modest growth of algae which fed local plant eating fish. The ponds used natural tidal flushing to bring in fresh seawater and remove waste, which kept oxygen levels stable. And here's the clever part. The special sluice gates connecting the ponds to the ocean had small holes. These holes allowed juvenile fish to swim in from the ocean and fatten up on the food in the pond, but then prevented them from escaping once they matured so they could be easily harvested.
records.translation:
食物加上废弃物会引发藻华吗？
藻华是藻类（一种微小的水生植物，能使水变得浑浊）的迅速增殖。
当这些藻华死亡时，它们会分解并消耗水中的氧气，这可能导致鱼类和其他水生生物窒息。
当然，藻华的主要原因是农业径流中的化学肥料，比如雨水或灌溉水流经田地，将肥料带入河流和沿海水域。
但养鱼业也会导致藻华。
一个有趣的替代方案是或曾经是古夏威夷的沿海鱼塘，叫做Lokoiya。
今天夏威夷的人们正在复兴它们。
这些池塘主要利用熔岩沿海岸建造，捕获了附近田地富含营养的径流，天然地滋养了池塘。
这发生在浓缩人造肥料出现之前。
这些营养物质没有引起藻华，而是支持了藻类的适度生长，这些藻类喂养了当地的食草鱼类。
池塘利用自然的潮汐冲刷引入新鲜海水并清除废物，从而保持了氧气水平的稳定。
而这正是巧妙之处。
连接池塘与海洋的特殊水闸门有小孔。
这些小孔允许幼鱼从海洋游入池塘并在池塘中觅食长胖，但当它们成熟后，又阻止它们逃脱，这样它们就可以被轻松捕捞了。

transcriptSentences.text: Can food plus waste products trigger algal blooms?
Algal blooms are rapid increases in algae, tiny aquatic plants that can cloud the water.
When those algal blooms die off, they decompose and deplete oxygen from the water, which can suffocate fish and other aquatic life.

Of course, the main cause of algal blooms is chemical fertilizers in agricultural runoff, like when water from rain or irrigation flows over fields and carries the fertilizers to rivers and coastal waters.
But fish farming causes algal blooms too.
An intriguing alternative is or was the coastal fish ponds of ancient Hawaii called Lokoiya.
People in Hawaii are reviving them today.
These ponds, built along the shore using mainly lava, captured nutrient rich runoff from nearby fields, naturally fertilizing the ponds.
This was before the days of concentrated artificial fertilizers.
Instead of causing algal blooms, the nutrients supported modest growth of algae which fed local plant eating fish.
The ponds used natural tidal flushing to bring in fresh seawater and remove waste, which kept oxygen levels stable.
And here's the clever part.
The special sluice gates connecting the ponds to the ocean had small holes.
These holes allowed juvenile fish to swim in from the ocean and fatten up on the food in the pond, but then prevented them from escaping once they matured so they could be easily harvested.

records.transcript: Imagine an animal so well protected that even a hungry tiger walks away frustrated. Meet the Indian pangolin, a nocturnal mammal covered in overlapping scales that act like a suit of armor. These scales are made of keratin, the same protein found in human fingernails. They're a powerful defense mechanism. When it encounters an enemy, the pangolin performs volvation, curling into a tight ball, providing itself with an impenetrable shield. This remarkable use of volvation makes pangolins exceptional among mammals. Few other creatures can achieve such a complete protective posture. Pangolins also have strong claws for digging and a long, sticky tongue that can extend up to 25 centimeters, perfect for capturing ants and termites. They lack teeth, so instead of chewing, they grind their food in their stomach. Their stomach is lined with keratin plates, similar to their outer scales. These plates are extremely hard and work together with the contractions of the stomach to crush and grind captured prey. Now, although the Indian pangolin's armor deters most predators, tigers, leopards, and hyenas occasionally manage to pry them open. Still, the greatest threat to the Indian pangolin is illegal hunting for scales and meat, which, along with habitat destruction, have pushed it toward endangered status. Why does this matter? Well, pangolins are ecological guardians. By consuming millions of insects, they prevent pest outbreaks that could harm crops and forests. Their digging also helps air get into the soil, improving plant health. Losing pangolins would disrupt these processes, creating ripple effects across various ecosystems.
records.translation:
想象一种动物，它受到了很好的保护，即使是饥饿的老虎也会沮丧地走开。
认识一下印度穿山甲，一种夜间活动的哺乳动物，身上覆盖着重叠的鳞片，就像一套盔甲。
这些鳞片由角蛋白构成，与人类指甲中的蛋白质相同。
它们是一种强大的防御机制。
当遇到敌人时，穿山甲会进行“卷曲”，蜷缩成一个紧密的球，为自己提供一个坚不可摧的盾牌。
这种非凡的卷曲方式使穿山甲在哺乳动物中独树一帜。
很少有其他生物能达到如此完整的保护姿态。
穿山甲还有强壮的爪子用于挖掘，以及一条可以伸长达25厘米的粘性长舌，非常适合捕捉蚂蚁和白蚁。
它们没有牙齿，所以不咀嚼，而是在胃里磨碎食物。
它们的胃内壁衬有角蛋白板，类似于它们的外层鳞片。
这些板非常坚硬，与胃的收缩一起工作，以粉碎和磨碎捕获的猎物。
现在，尽管印度穿山甲的盔甲能威慑大多数捕食者，但老虎、豹子和鬣狗偶尔也能将其撬开。
然而，印度穿山甲面临的最大威胁是为获取鳞片和肉而进行的非法狩猎，这与栖息地破坏一起，已将其推向濒危状态。
为什么这很重要？
嗯，穿山甲是生态的守护者。
通过消耗数百万昆虫，它们可以防止可能损害农作物和森林的害虫爆发。
它们的挖掘也有助于空气进入土壤，改善植物健康。
失去穿山甲将破坏这些过程，在各种生态系统中产生连锁反应。

transcriptSentences.text: Imagine an animal so well protected that even a hungry tiger walks away frustrated.
Meet the Indian pangolin, a nocturnal mammal covered in overlapping scales that act like a suit of armor.
These scales are made of keratin, the same protein found in human fingernails.
They're a powerful defense mechanism.
When it encounters an enemy, the pangolin performs volvation, curling into a tight ball, providing itself with an impenetrable shield.
This remarkable use of volvation makes pangolins exceptional among mammals.
Few other creatures can achieve such a complete protective posture.
Pangolins also have strong claws for digging and a long, sticky tongue that can extend up to 25 centimeters, perfect for capturing ants and termites.
They lack teeth, so instead of chewing, they grind their food in their stomach.
Their stomach is lined with keratin plates, similar to their outer scales.
These plates are extremely hard and work together with the contractions of the stomach to crush and grind captured prey.
Now, although the Indian pangolin's armor deters most predators, tigers, leopards, and hyenas occasionally manage to pry them open.
Still, the greatest threat to the Indian pangolin is illegal hunting for scales and meat, which, along with habitat destruction, have pushed it toward endangered status.
Why does this matter?
Well, pangolins are ecological guardians.
By consuming millions of insects, they prevent pest outbreaks that could harm crops and forests.
Their digging also helps air get into the soil, improving plant health.
Losing pangolins would disrupt these processes, creating ripple effects across various ecosystems.
